## Abstract

Quantum computing poses a serious threat to classical cryptographic algorithms based on computational complexity. Quantum key distribution (QKD), utilizing the principles of quantum mechanics, enables secure key exchange and has been proven to be an essential technology to resist the threat of quantum computing. China attaches great importance to the construction of QKD network to deal with this threat. In 2020, China established an integrated space-to-ground quantum communication network, which includes 32 backbone nodes and 4 metropolitan networks. Here we introduce China’s latest progress in the deployment of QKD networks, called the China Quantum Communication Network (CN-QCN). CN-QCN is an operational, long-range, and trusted-relay-based QKD network spanning over 10,000 kilometers, incorporating 145 fiber backbone nodes, and 20 metropolitan networks, which cover 17 provinces and 80 cities. Moreover, the network has deployed 6 ground stations linked with Jinan-1 quantum microsatellite. CN-QCN has not only surpassed its predecessor in scale, but also made significant advancements in multi-type QKD hybrid networking and long-range quantum network operation and maintenance. We present the network architecture, QKD implementation, and long-term performance of CN-QCN in this paper. This work lays the foundation for widespread applications of QKD in China.

## Introduction

As a countermeasure against quantum computing threats, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)[1](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR1 "Bennett, C. H. & Brassard, G. Quantum cryptography: public key distribution and coin tossing. In Proc. IEEE International Conference on Computers, Systems, and Signal Processing 175-179 (IEEE, New York, 1984)."), provides a robust solution by enabling distant parties to establish a shared secret key with information-theoretic security. Over the past four decades, QKD technology has made significant progress in achieving longer transmission distances, higher secure key rate, and improved practical security. The transmission distance has increased from an initial 32 cm[2](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR2 "Bennett, C. H., Bessette, F., Brassard, G., Salvail, L. & Smolin, J. Experimental quantum cryptography. J. Cryptol. 5, 3–28 (1992).") in laboratory experiments to over 1000 km[3](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR3 "Liu, Y. et al. Experimental twin-field quantum key distribution over 1000 km fiber distance. Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 210801 (2023)."),[4](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR4 "Liu, Y. et al. 1002 km twin-field quantum key distribution with finite-key analysis. Quantum Front. 2, 16 (2023)."). On a separate front, secure key rates have also seen dramatic improvements, now exceeding 100 Mbps in high-performance setups[5](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR5 "Li, W. et al. High-rate quantum key distribution exceeding 110 Mb s–1. Nat. Photon. 17, 416–421 (2023)."). Simultaneously, a comprehensive practical security protocol framework has been systematically established and implemented[6](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR6 "Xu, F., Ma, X., Zhang, Q., Lo, H.-K. & Pan, J.-W. Secure quantum key distribution with realistic devices. Rev. Mod. Phys. 92, 025002 (2020).").

Many countries and regions around the world have launched field tests of QKD networks, including DAPRA’s three-user network (2003)[7](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR7 "Elliott, C. et al. Current status of the DARPA quantum network. In Quantum Information and Computation III Vol. 5815, 138–150 (International Society for Optics and Photonics, 2005)."), the six-node SECOQC network in Austria (2008)[8](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR8 "Peev, M. et al. The SECOQC quantum key distribution network in Vienna. N. J. Phys. 11, 075001 (2009)."), the Swiss QKD network featuring three-node key management functionality (2009)[9](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR9 "Stucki, D. et al. Long-term performance of the SwissQuantum quantum key distribution network in a field environment. N. J. Phys. 13, 123001 (2011)."), the six-node mesh-type network in Tokyo (2010)[10](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR10 "Sasaki, M. et al. Field test of quantum key distribution in the Tokyo QKD Network. Opt. Express 19, 10387 (2011)."), the three-node high-speed quantum metropolitan ring network in Cambridge (2019)[11](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR11 "Dynes, J. F. et al. Cambridge quantum network. npj Quantum Inf. 5, 101 (2019)."), the 46-node quantum metropolitan network in Hefei (2021)[12](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR12 "Chen, T. Y. et al. Implementation of a 46-node quantum metropolitan area network. npj Quantum Inf. 7, 134 (2021)."), etc. For long-distance backbone QKD networks, China initiated the construction of the world’s first long-distance quantum backbone network, the Beijing-Shanghai Backbone Network (BSBN), in 2013. The network was completed by 2017, spanning 2032 km and comprising 32 nodes. In 2020, BSBN established a satellite-to-ground link with the Micius satellite, creating the world’s first integrated satellite-ground quantum secure communication network, spanning of 4600 km[13](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR13 "Chen, Y.-A. et al. An integrated space-to-ground quantum communication network over 4600 kilometers. Nature 589, 214–219 (2021)."). The European Union launched the OPENQKD project in June 2019 and constructed QKD network exceeding 1000 kilometers[14](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR14 "European Union. CORDIS - EU research results. 
                  https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/857156
                  
                 (2024)."). Base on OPENQKD project, the European Union began the construction of European Quantum Communication Infrastructure (EuroQCI), where MadQCI has been deployed using Software-Defined Networking (SDN) in Spain (2024)[15](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR15 "Martin, V. et al. MadQCI: a heterogeneous and scalable SDN-QKD network deployed in production facilities. npj Quantum Inf. 10, 80 (2024).") and interconnection tests between remote QKD networks has been conducted in Berlin, Madrid, and Poznan (2024)[16](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR16 "Brauer, M. et al. Linking QKD Testbeds across Europe. Entropy 26, 123 (2024).").

To achieve more reliable, secure, and long-range key distribution, and to facilitate the transition of quantum networks from technology verification networks to carrier-grade networks, China has launched the national quantum communication network project (CN-QCN). Compared to BSBN, CN-QCN significantly expands its coverage by newly constructing 145 fiber backbone nodes, 6 ground station backbone nodes, 20 metropolitan networks, and an operations and maintenance (O&M) center, extending across 17 provinces and 80 cities. CN-QCN is interconnected with BSBN, and the combined fiber mileage of the two exceeds 12,000 kilometers, making it the largest quantum network in the world to date. In this paper, we present the network topology and architecture of CN-QCN. Subsequently, we focus on the technical solutions and key generation performance of different types of QKD devices deployed in the backbone and metropolitan networks. Finally, we analyze the long-term operational status of CN-QCN.

## Results

### Network topology

CN-QCN consists of several backbone networks and metropolitan networks. Spanning across China’s principal urban centers, the backbone network operates in coordination with BSBN to implement a distinctive “two-horizontal, two-vertical” topological framework that optimizes nationwide connectivity. Notably, Beijing, Jinan, Hefei, and Wuhan, as well as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Hefei, and Nanjing form two ring structures, enabling ring-topology protection within the QKD network. The backbone network comprises 145 fiber backbone nodes and 144 fiber links, with a total optical fiber length of approximately 10,103 km. The average distance between adjacent QKD nodes is about 70 km, with an average attenuation of 18.61 dB per link. Among the 145 backbone nodes, 41 are designated as backbone access nodes with metropolitan network access capabilities, while the remaining 104 nodes serve as relay nodes. As illustrated in Fig. [1](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#Fig1), the green lines represent CN-QCN backbone links, the yellow lines indicate BSBN, and the red circles denote backbone access nodes, which are capable of interfacing with metropolitan networks and performing key relaying in multiple directions. The yellow dots represent trusted relay nodes located between backbone access nodes, each responsible for key forwarding to neighboring nodes.

**Fig. 1: Network topology.**

![Fig. 1: Network topology.](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41534-025-01089-8/MediaObjects/41534_2025_1089_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8/figures/1)

The backbone network comprises CN-QCN (green lines) and BSBN (yellow lines). There are 145 backbone nodes, 41 (red circles) are backbone access nodes, while the remaining 104 nodes are relay nodes (yellow dots). The blue circle denotes the O&M center. In the metropolitan network, the blue dots indicate metropolitan access nodes, and green dots represent user nodes. The quantum microsatellite can connect to ground stations.

Some backbone access nodes are connected to metropolitan networks. Metropolitan networks enable users within a metropolitan region to access the QKD network and establish cross-regional interconnections via the backbone. Depending on the city scale and user distribution, several access nodes are deployed in each metropolitan network. The metropolitan access nodes are interconnected using ring or chain topologies, while the links from access nodes to user nodes adopt a tree topology. Each user node can provide quantum keys to multiple end user systems. We have deployed QKD devices and optical switches at each metropolitan access node to enable time-division multiplexing (TDM) for different user nodes. Each optical switch supports switching for up to 24 user nodes. To date, metropolitan networks have been deployed in 20 cities including Beijing, Shanghai, Jinhua, Haikou, and Chongqing, comprising 36 access nodes which are able to support more than 800 user nodes. These access nodes can be upgraded and expanded according to user demands.

The backbone nodes in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chongqing, Hainan, and Xinjiang are equipped with satellite ground stations. Through the Jinan-1 quantum microsatellite, key relays are established to create KM links, thereby interconnecting the satellite-ground and fiber-based QKD infrastructures. The detailed information about the Jinan-1 quantum microsatellite can be found in ref. [17](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR17 "Li, Y. et al. Microsatellite-based real-time quantum key distribution. Nature 640, 47–54 (2025).").

An operation and maintenance (O&M) center has been established for the entire QKD network. It performs real-time collection of QKD performance indicators such as secure key rate, quantum bit error rate, KM-Links status, etc. It also monitors the physical environment of equipment rooms and the operation status of classical communication systems, ensuring 24/7 maintenance services for the quantum network.

To ensure the long-term stability and security of CN-QCN, the network not only uses independent server room spaces and dark fiber resources, but also deploys exclusive equipment, including Optical Transport Network (OTN) devices, Network Time Protocol (NTP) servers, network security devices and so on. These measures ensure strict network isolation between CN-QCN and the Internet, preventing information leakage and cyber-attacks. We present deployment schematics for several representative nodes in Supplementary Note [1](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1).

### Network architecture

The functional architecture of CN-QCN comprises the quantum layer, key management layer, QKD network control layer, QKD network management layer, and application layer (Fig. [2](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#Fig2)), in accordance with the ITU-T Y.3802 recommendation Quantum Key Distribution Networks—Functional Architecture[18](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR18 "ITU-T Y.3802. Quantum key distribution networks – Functional architecture[S] (2020)."). In the quantum layer, QKD-links utilize either the decoy-state BB84 protocol[19](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR19 "Ma, X., Qi, B., Zhao, Y. & Lo, H.-K. Practical decoy state for quantum key distribution. Phys. Rev. A 72, 012326 (2005).") or Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable (CV) QKD protocols[20](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR20 "Grosshans, F. & Grangier, P. Continuous variable quantum cryptography using coherent states. Phys. Rev. Lett. 88, 057902 (2002)."),[21](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR21 "Weedbrook, C. et al. Quantum cryptography without switching. Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 170504 (2004).") to generate QKD-keys between two adjacent nodes which are subsequently delivered to the key management layer. Wavelength division multiplexers (WDM) or optical switches (OS) are used for multiplexing quantum channels. The key management layer performs key relaying based on the One-Time-Pad scheme, establishing key management links (KM-Links) between two arbitrary nodes to enable end-to-end, networked key distribution and provide key services to end user systems. Notably, each KM-Link may utilize one or more underlying QKD-Links. These KM-Links can establish both direct connections between adjacent nodes and remote connections between non-adjacent nodes via predefined key relay paths. The QKD network control layer is responsible for key routing calculation and control. It gathers real-time data on the key quantity of each KM-link, computes the optimum key relay paths according to the demand of key services and dispatches key relay policies to the corresponding KM devices. The control layer adopts a hierarchical architecture: Level-1 QKD network controllers are in charge of inter-domain routing between backbone and metropolitan networks within a given region, while Level-2 QKDN controllers are responsible for intra-domain routing of one backbone or metropolitan network. If there is a need for key relaying between different regional networks, the corresponding Level-1 controllers should coordinate the routing processes. The QKD network management layer also follows a hierarchical deployment model. The element management system (EMS) in each region collects device status from local network elements and transmits the information via northbound interfaces to the centralized network management system (NMS) located at the O&M center. This facilitates real-time status monitoring of the entire network.

**Fig. 2: Functional architecture of the QKD network.**

![Fig. 2: Functional architecture of the QKD network.](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41534-025-01089-8/MediaObjects/41534_2025_1089_Fig2_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8/figures/2)

The network consists of five layers: the quantum layer, the key management layer, the QKD network control layer, the QKD network management layer and the application layer. The quantum layer is responsible for key distribution between two adjacent nodes. The key management layer performs key relaying based on the One-Time-Pad scheme to complete an end-to-end key distribution. The QKD network control layer is responsible for key routing calculation and control. The QKD network management layer monitors the network status. The application layer uses the secure keys for encryption and authentication. Definitions of abbreviations, QKD: Quantum Key Distribution device; WDM: Wavelength division multiplexers; OS: Optical Switch; KM: Key Manager; QKDN-C: QKD Network Controller; EMS: Element Management System; NMS: Network Management System; User: End User System.

### QKD implementation

In backbone networks, we have deployed four distinct high-speed QKD systems, all adhering to the decoy-state BB84 protocol. Three of these systems are polarization-encoding systems operating at a repetition frequency of 625 MHz (labeled as Types I, II, and III), and the other one is a phase-encoding system operating at a repetition frequency of 312.5 MHz (labeled as Type IV). Type I incorporates a single-laser scheme (for details, see Supplementary Fig. [2](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1)). In this scheme, the laser at the transmitter emits optical pulses that are modulated into decoy states by an intensity modulator, followed by a polarization encoding module to achieve modulation of four polarization states. At the receiver side, four InGaAs/InP single-photon detectors with a detection efficiency of 15% are utilized. Type II and Type III transmitters share the same structure, both employing a multi-laser scheme (as detailed in Supplementary Fig. [3](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1)), utilizing eight lasers to achieve modulation of four polarization states for signal and decoy states. At the receiver side, Type II implements four up-conversion single-photon detectors with a detection efficiency of 20%, whereas Type III utilizes four InGaAs/InP single-photon detectors with a detection efficiency of 10%. In the Type IV system (as illustrated in Supplementary Fig. [4](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1)), the transmitter primarily consists of two Sagnac interferometers and an asymmetric Mach-Zehnder interferometer, which together facilitate the intensity modulation and encoding of quantum states. The receiver employs a Faraday mirror-based Michelson interferometer for decoding, with a detection efficiency of 15%.

These QKD devices account for the primary quantum hacking strategies and have been designed with corresponding countermeasures. For instance, the decoy-state protocol has been implemented to counter photon-number-splitting attacks[22](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR22 "Brassard, G., Lütkenhaus, N., Mor, T. & Sanders, B. C. Limitations on practical quantum cryptography. Phys. Rev. Lett. 85, 1330–1333 (2000)."); the transmitter of the QKD system is equipped with optical circulators to achieve high isolation, preventing Trojan-horse attacks[23](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR23 "Lucamarini, M. et al. Practical security bounds against the Trejan-Hose attack in quantum key distribution. Phys. Rev. X 5, 031030-1-19 (2015).") and laser seeding attacks[24](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR24 "Sun, S.-H. et al. Effect of source tampering in the security of quantum cryptography. Phys. Rev. A 92, 022304 (2015)."). The receiver is safeguarded against time-shift attacks[25](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR25 "Qi, B., Fung, C.-H. F., Lo, H.-K. & Ma, X. Time-shift attack in practical quantum cryptosystems. Quantum Inf. Comput. 7, 73–82 (2007).") by precisely setting the detector delays. Also, an electrical monitor is included for real-time monitoring of the output current from the single-photon detectors, to counter detector blinding attacks[26](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR26 "Lydersen, L. et al. Hacking commercial quantum cryptography systems by tailored bright illumination. Nat. Photon. 4, 686–689 (2010)."). Compared to multi-laser schemes, the single-laser scheme further prevents side-channel attacks that arise from the inability to maintain complete consistency in the attributes of laser wavelength, temporal characteristics and so on[27](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR27 "Gnanapandithan, A., Qian, L. & Lo, H.-K. Hidden multidimensional modulation side channels in quantum protocols. Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 130802 (2025).").

Although the same type of QKD systems follow identical technical standards, variations in the performance of components and operating environments can still lead to differences in the secure key rates. For instance, the intrinsic quantum bit error rate may vary from 0.5% to 2% in actual environments, the dark count rate for single-photon detectors generally ranges between 600 Hz and 1000 Hz, and the error correction efficiency typically ranges from 1.2 to 2. Furthermore, the methods for calculating the secure key rate exhibit slight differences among various types of devices. Supplementary Note [2](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1) details the system architecture, typical parameters, and secure key rate calculation method for each QKD system types.

Figure [3](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#Fig3) illustrates the relationship between the single-pair secure key rate and quantum channel loss in the backbone network. To avoid redundant statistics under identical conditions, the figure includes data from only one pair of QKD systems selected from multiple pairs of the same type of QKD systems deployed in the same fiber link. To accurately assess the discrepancies between the actual and theoretical secure key rates, we plotted the single-pair secure key rates for identical types of QKD systems on the same graph. Subsequently, we simulated the relationship between the secure key rate and channel loss using ideal system parameters, which include an intrinsic error rate of 0.5%, a dark count rate of 600 Hz, and an error correction efficiency of 1.2. The results indicate that the actual secure key rate is lower than the theoretical value, attributable to several factors: variations in device performance due to differences in manufacturing processes; in practical applications, QKD systems are affected by temperature fluctuations and fiber vibrations, leading to reduced quantum channel stability and increased error rates; synchronization light leakage increases the noise; and fluctuations in error rates limit the optimal parameter selection for error correction algorithms, thereby reducing the efficiency of error correction. Collectively, these factors contribute to the reduction in the actual secure key rate. Nonetheless, the trend of the actual secure key rate remains consistent with the theoretical simulation results, and QKD devices operate within the linear range where the secure key rate is linearly related to the channel transmittance.

In metropolitan networks, where fiber link loss is relatively low, we have deployed a low-speed QKD system based on the decoy-state BB84 protocol (labeled as Type V), as well as two types of CV-QKD devices based on Gaussian-modulated coherent states (labeled as Types VI and VII). Type V QKD systems utilize a single-laser scheme, featuring an optical structure similar to that of Type I, operating at a repetition frequency of 40 MHz, with an intrinsic error rate ranging from 0.5% to 2%, and a detection efficiency of 10%. Type VI CV-QKD systems employ a locally-generated local oscillator (LLO) scheme, wherein the transmitter employs IQ modulation technology with a modulation variance set to 4 and a repetition frequency of 125 MHz. At the receiver, after heterodyne detection of the quantum signal and LO, bit information is yielded, with a quantum efficiency of approximately 0.43 and an electrical noise variance of about 0.2 (SNU). Type VII systems adopt a transmitted local oscillator (TLO) scheme, with a modulation variance set to 4 and a modulation rate of 10 MHz. In contrast to the LLO scheme, the TLO scheme generates the LO and quantum signal light from the same laser, which are then time and polarization multiplexed using an isolate polarization beam splitter. At the receiver, a homodyne detection scheme is employed, with a quantum efficiency of 0.6 and an electrical noise variance of approximately 0.13. Details of the system structures for Types V, VI, and VII can be found in Supplementary Note [2](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#MOESM1). ### Network reliability and security

To evaluate the secure key rate performance of the backbone network, we selected the backbone network from Harbin to Shenzhen and conducted statistics over a period of 10 weeks. As shown in Fig. [5a](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#Fig5), we present the average secure key rates of all adjacent KM-Links between Harbin and Shenzhen over this period. Among the 64 KM-Links, the minimum secure key rate was 9.75 kbps, and the maximum was 359.89 kbps. Furthermore, we segmented the link from Harbin to Shenzhen into four segments: Harbin to Beijing, Beijing to Wuhan, Wuhan to Guangzhou, and Guangzhou to Shenzhen. For each segment, the end-to-end secure key rate is determined by the minimum secure key rate among all KM-Links between adjacent nodes. The average end-to-end secure key rates for the four segments were 9.75 kbps, 16.41 kbps, 20.73 kbps, and 20.85 kbps, respectively. We also calculated the weekly average end-to-end secure key rates for these segments and depicted their variations over this period, as illustrated in Fig. [5b](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#Fig5). The experimental results demonstrate that all segments sustained consistent secure key rates throughout the extended operation period.

It records the service interruption durations for each of the four network segments on a weekly basis over the ten-week observation period. The results show that KM-Links from Beijing to Wuhan were always available due to the existence of redundant routing paths. In contrast, single-link topologies are more vulnerable to disruptions because of the interruption of any fiber link or the equipment failure of one node, for instance, the KM-Links from Harbin to Beijing and from Wuhan to Guangzhou. Therefore, ring-topology protection is particularly necessary for long-distance QKD backbones.

Besides, during the construction of CN-QCN, particular emphasis was placed on the overall security of the network to ensure compliance with general security standards. This is especially critical because layers above the quantum layer are no longer inherently protected by the principles of quantum mechanics. Compared to BSBN, CN-QCN incorporates more comprehensive technical safeguards and stricter management practices across five layers: physical environment, network communication, device software, application data, and security management. For example, stringent physical access control mechanisms were implemented to secure trusted relay nodes. These measures collectively enable CN-QCN to support large-scale applications in sectors such as government, finance, and energy.

## Discussion

In summary, this paper presents a carrier-grade quantum communication network developed in China, comprising over 10,000 km of optical fiber links, which represents an important milestone in the development of the global quantum communication network. CN-QCN has not only surpassed BSBN in scale, but also made significant advancements in multi-type QKD hybrid networking and long-range quantum network operation and maintenance. We illustrate the topology and architecture of the network, and explain the actual deployment and the main business processes of the network. We focus on the technical solutions and key generation status of the 7 types of QKD devices deployed in the backbone and metropolitan networks. Finally, we examine the secure key rate and availability of the network during long-term operation, which demonstrates the stability and robustness of the network operation. We hold the view that CN-QCN will become an important information security infrastructure in China, laying the foundation for countering the threat of quantum computing. In the future, with the development of quantum measurement[28](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR28 "Komar, P. et al. A quantum network of clocks. Nat. Phys. 10, 582–587 (2014).") and quantum relay[29](/articles/s41534-025-01089-8#ref-CR29 "Briegel, H. J., Dür, W., Cirac, J. I. & Zoller, P. Quantum repeaters: the role of imperfect local operations in quantum communication. Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932–5935 (1998).") technologies, this network can also serve as a testbed and incubator for various quantum information technologies, paving the way for the development of the quantum internet.

args.summary:
This paper presents the China Quantum Communication Network (CN-QCN), an operational carrier-grade quantum key distribution (QKD) network spanning over 10,000 km. It is a trusted-relay-based QKD network incorporating 145 fiber backbone nodes, 20 metropolitan networks, covering 17 provinces and 80 cities, and 6 ground stations linked with the Jinan-1 quantum microsatellite. Combined with the earlier Beijing-Shanghai Backbone Network (BSBN), the total fiber mileage exceeds 12,000 km, making it the largest quantum network in the world to date.

The network employs a "two-horizontal, two-vertical" topological framework with ring-topology protection. The backbone network features 145 fiber backbone nodes and 144 fiber links (total ~10,103 km), with average inter-node distance of ~70 km and average attenuation of 18.61 dB per link. Of the 145 backbone nodes, 41 are backbone access nodes with metropolitan network access capabilities. Metropolitan networks have been deployed in 20 cities, comprising 36 access nodes supporting more than 800 user nodes.

The network architecture follows ITU-T Y.3802 and comprises five layers: quantum layer, key management layer, QKD network control layer, QKD network management layer, and application layer. The control layer uses a hierarchical architecture with Level-1 and Level-2 controllers.

Seven types of QKD devices are deployed: four high-speed systems (Types I-IV) in backbone networks based on the decoy-state BB84 protocol, and three metropolitan systems (Types V-VII) including both discrete-variable and continuous-variable (CV-QKD) approaches. The backbone systems operate at 625 MHz (Types I-III) or 312.5 MHz (Type IV). Security countermeasures are implemented against photon-number-splitting attacks, Trojan-horse attacks, laser seeding attacks, time-shift attacks, and detector blinding attacks.

Long-term performance evaluation over a 10-week period on the Harbin-Shenzhen backbone path (64 KM-Links) showed minimum secure key rate of 9.75 kbps and maximum of 359.89 kbps. The network demonstrated consistent secure key rates throughout extended operation, and ring-topology protection was found to be particularly necessary for resilience against disruptions.

The paper concludes that CN-QCN will become an important information security infrastructure in China, and can serve as a testbed for future quantum internet technologies including quantum measurement and quantum relay.

# QKD Net­work Imple­men­ta­ti­on across 10,000 Kilo­me­ters

![](https://www.squad-germany.de/ycickowu/2025/08/CN-QCN-1024x607.png)

## Chi­na imple­ments CN-QCN as a Long-Ran­ge Quan­tum Com­mu­ni­ca­ti­on Net­work:

The rapid deve­lo­p­ment of Quan­tum Com­pu­ters poses a serious thre­at to clas­si­cal encryp­ti­on methods, which rely on the com­ple­xi­ty of mathe­ma­ti­cal func­tions. Due to their enorm­ous com­pu­ta­tio­nal power, Quan­tum Com­pu­ters can break curr­ent­ly used algo­rith­ms in a very short time. This is exact­ly whe­re Quan­tum Com­mu­ni­ca­ti­on comes in: it offers enti­re­ly new and secu­re ways of trans­mit­ting data. Quan­tum Key Dis­tri­bu­ti­on (QKD), which lever­a­ges the prin­ci­ples of Quan­tum Mecha­nics, enables secu­re key exch­an­ge and has pro­ven to be a ground­brea­king tech­no­lo­gy to coun­ter the thre­at posed by Quan­tum Com­pu­ters.

Against this back­drop, Chi­na estab­lished an inte­gra­ted space-to-ground Quan­tum Com­mu­ni­ca­ti­on Net­work in 2020, initi­al­ly com­pri­sing 32 back­bone nodes and four metro­po­li­tan net­works. The latest advan­ces in the deve­lo­p­ment of the so-cal­led Chi­na Quan­tum Com­mu­ni­ca­ti­on Net­work (CN-QCN) have now been pre­sen­ted in a new [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41534-025-01089-8?utm_source=nature_etoc&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=CONR_41534_AWA1_GL_DTEC_054CI_TOC-250827&utm_content=20250827). CN-QCN is an ope­ra­tio­nal, long-ran­ge QKD net­work based on trus­ted relays, span­ning over 10,000 kilo­me­ters. It con­sists of 145 fiber back­bone nodes and 20 metro­po­li­tan net­works cove­ring 17 pro­vin­ces and 80 cities, as well as 6 ground sta­ti­ons lin­ked with the Quan­tum micro­sa­tel­li­te Jinan‑1.

CN-QCN not only sur­pas­ses its pre­de­ces­sor, the Bei­jing-Shang­hai Back­bone Net­work (BSBN), but also achie­ves signi­fi­cant advan­ces in mul­ti-type QKD hybrid net­wor­king, as well as in the ope­ra­ti­on and main­ten­an­ce of lar­ge-sca­le Quan­tum Net­works. The new artic­le details the net­work archi­tec­tu­re, the QKD imple­men­ta­ti­on, and the long-term per­for­mance of CN-QCN, lay­ing the foun­da­ti­on for the wide­spread appli­ca­ti­on of QKD in Chi­na.

Source refe­rence: [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41534-025–01089‑8?utm\_source=nature\_etoc&utm\_medium=email&utm\_campaign=CONR\_41534\_AWA1\_GL\_DTEC\_054CI\_TOC-250827&utm\_content=20250827](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41534-025-01089-8?utm_source=nature_etoc&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=CONR_41534_AWA1_GL_DTEC_054CI_TOC-250827&utm_content=20250827)

# China’s 2,000-km Quantum Link Is Almost Complete

## The Beijing-Shanghai project will form the backbone of the nation’s quantum communications network

[Rachel Courtland](https://spectrum.ieee.org/u/rachel-courtland)

26 Oct 2016

4 min read

Quantum Space Link: Staff work on China’s quantum research satellite, which launched in August. It is part of a larger effort in the country to push the limits of quantum key distribution.

Photo: Xinhua/Alamy

By the end of this year, ateam led by researchers from the [University of Science and Technology of China](https://en.ustc.edu.cn/), in Hefei, aims to put the finishing touches on a 2,000-kilometer-long fiber-optic link that will wind its way from Beijing in the north to the coastal city of [Shanghai](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/shanghai).

What will distinguish this particular stretch of fiber from myriad other long-distance links is its intended application: the exchange of quantum keys for secure communication—a sophisticated gambit to protect data from present and future hackers. If all goes according to plan, this Beijing–Shanghai line will connect [quantum networks](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/quantum-networks) in four cities. And this large-scale terrestrial effort now has a partner in space: A quantum science satellite was launched in August with a research mission that includes testing the distribution of keys well beyond the country’s borders.

With these developments, [China](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/china) is poised to vastly extend the reach of [quantum key distribution](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/quantum-key-distribution) (QKD), an approach for creating shared cryptographic keys—sequences of random bits—that can be used to encrypt and decrypt data. Thanks to the fundamental nature of quantum mechanics, QKD has the distinction of being, in principle, unhackable. A malicious party that attempts to eavesdrop on a quantum transmission won’t be able to do so without creating detectable errors.

QKD has already made its way into the real world. In 2007, the scheme was used to [secure the transmission of votes](/computing/networks/geneva-vote-will-use-quantum-cryptography) in a Swiss [election](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/election). Several years ago, the U.S.-based firm [Battelle](https://www.battelle.org/about-us) began to use the approach to exchange information securely over kilometers of fiber between its corporate headquarters in Columbus, Ohio, and a production facility in Dublin, Ohio.

But despite great progress, there has been a stumbling block to wide distribution. “The problem we’ve got is distance,” says [Tim Spiller,](https://www.york.ac.uk/physics/people/spiller/) director of the United Kingdom’s [Quantum Communications](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/quantum-communications) Hub, a nationally funded project that is building and connecting quantum networks in Bristol and Cambridge, in England.

The challenge is that QKD encodes information in the states of individual photons. And those photons can’t travel indefinitely in fiber or through the air; the longer the distance, the greater the chance they will be absorbed or scattered.

This characteristic has a direct impact on how quickly a quantum key can be generated, explains physicist Jian-Wei Pan, who leads the Chinese projects. If researchers attempted to send signals directly down 1,000 kilometers of fiber, Pan says, “even using all the best technology, we would only manage to send 1 bit of secure key over 300 years.”

Instead, QKD fiber links must have a way to refresh the signal every 100 km or so to maintain a reasonable bit rate. But this can’t be done with conventional telecommunications equipment. The same rules that protect quantum transmission against eavesdropping also prohibit a quantum key from being copied without corrupting it. The solution has been to concatenate, creating a daisy chain of individual quantum links connected by physically secured spots, or “trusted nodes.” Each intermediate node measures the key and then transmits it with fresh photons to the next node in the chain.

Illustration: Erik Vrielink

**River of Secrets:** A 2,000-kilometer-long backbone will connect quantum networks in four cities. The line uses a number of secured nodes as relays along the route.

The Beijing–Shanghai line will use 32  trusted nodes to create the 2,000-km line. This approach isn’t ideal for security. Because each trusted node has to convert the quantum key back into classical (nonquantum) information before passing it on, an eavesdropper at the node could potentially hack the data stream there undetected. “That’s the drawback,” Pan says. But the approach is “still much better than traditional communications… [where] there is the possibility of performing eavesdropping” at every point along the route, he says. Here, the problem is limited to 32 spots under lock and key.

“A long-distance chain link like this, [it’s] really the first time it’s been done,” says Grégoire Ribordy of [ID Quantique](https://www.idquantique.com/), based in Geneva, which makes hardware for QKD networks. “It’s inspiring other people to try to do similar things around the world.”

If you want to avoid even the small vulnerability of trusted nodes, Spiller says, long-distance QKD must use quantum [entanglement](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/entanglement), a property that can link the states of photons separated by great physical distance and that can be exchanged between photons. “Quantum repeaters,” used in place of trusted nodes, could take advantage of this phenomenon to relay a quantum key without having to measure it. But this technology is still in an early stage of development, says Spiller; among other things, a quantum repeater will likely require a form of quantum memory to help coordinate communication.

“[If you] don’t have to trust any of the nodes along the network, that will broaden the applicability of QKD,” says Michele Mosca, cofounder of the Institute for [Quantum Computing](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/quantum-computing) at the University of Waterloo, in Ontario, Canada. One reason to improve QKD’s reach is to protect communications from tomorrow’s quantum computers, which could make short work of the public-key [cryptography](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/cryptography) that underpins Internet security and many other applications.

But Mosca notes that QKD is not the only possible way to address this threat; many cryptographers are exploring new “post-quantum” [algorithms](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/algorithms) to replace our existing public-key systems. QKD offers an “extra degree of assurance,” he says, but improved conventional cryptography will be a cheaper and more practical solution for many applications. Both will likely have a role to play in the coming years.

The interview covers his research in quantum error correction, quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum computing.

Key topics include: Jiang's work on quantum error correction to overcome practical imperfections; his role as an Amazon Scholar collaborating with AWS on quantum error correction; the challenges of achieving scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing (estimated timeline of a decade or longer); quantum transduction (converting quantum information between microwave and optical domains); quantum internet applications including secure communication, connecting quantum computers, and quantum telescopes; and his educational background at Caltech (undergraduate 2001-2004) and Harvard (PhD with Misha Lukin), followed by a post-doc at Caltech working with John Preskill.

Jiang discusses the fragility of quantum systems, the difficulty of quantum error correction (bit flip, dephasing, and leakage errors), and the progress made from fewer than 10 qubits to nearly 100 qubits with better fidelity. He compares different quantum computing platforms (trapped ions, superconducting qubits), discusses the competitive landscape among companies (Amazon, Google, IBM, Honeywell) and countries (US, China, Europe, Japan), and recounts his career trajectory from Caltech undergrad to Yale faculty to University of Chicago.

Notable achievements discussed include: the break-even performance of bosonic error correction demonstrated at Yale, his student Sisi Zhou solving a two-decade-old open problem about error correction and quantum sensing, and developments in quantum repeater schemes for long-distance quantum communication.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Harry Jeffrey Kimble (April 23, 1949 – September 2, 2024), known as Jeff Kimble, was a pioneering quantum physicist who made groundbreaking contributions to quantum optics and quantum information science. Born in Floydada, Texas, he attended Abilene Christian University on a basketball scholarship and earned his PhD from the University of Rochester in 1978 under Leonard Mandel, where he observed the first photon antibunching. He was a physics professor at UT Austin from 1979-1989, then joined Caltech from 1989 until his retirement in 2021, becoming the William L. Valentine Professor of Physics, Emeritus.

Kimble is best known for his pioneering work in cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED) and for the first high-fidelity demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1998, in which he teleported a beam of light (a quantum particle) across 2.7 meters. His experiments laid the foundations for quantum networks and the concept of a quantum internet. He co-founded the Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM) at Caltech and served as its inaugural director. He was a member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences and a fellow of Optica, AAAS, and APS. He received numerous awards including the Leonard Mandel Quantum Optics Award (2024), Herbert Walther Award (2013), Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize (2004), Albert A. Michelson Medal (1990), Einstein Prize for Laser Science (1989), and Optica's Max Born Award (1996).

Kimble was married to Margaret (Midge) Smith-Kimble for 45 years, with whom he had two daughters, Katherine and Megan. He was diagnosed with dementia in early 2023 and passed away at age 75 in Austin, Texas. He is survived by his wife, daughters, three granddaughters, and two brothers.
</summary>

URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2307.15696v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports on the comprehensive characterization of the Boston-Area Quantum Network (BARQNET), a 50-km fiber quantum network testbed connecting MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL), MIT, and Harvard University. The network comprises two 42.5 km fiber spans between MIT-LL and MIT, plus two additional 7.9 km spans between MIT and Harvard, using commercial telecom fibers (some buried, some above-ground).

Key characterization results include:

1. **Optical phase/frequency noise**: Phase fluctuations were orders of magnitude larger than those on buried fibers, requiring high-bandwidth stabilization (~650 kHz). The variance of optical frequency noise per fiber span was 5.74 kHz², with strong covariance (4.88 kHz²) between co-propagating fibers, suggesting phase-stable links benefit from distributed references. The phase drifts follow a Brownian diffusion model with variance per unit length of 133 Hz²/m.

2. **Polarization drift**: Measured over multiple days, polarization drift rates correlated strongly with wind speed (power law exponent ~1.74-1.87). Mean drift rates during high-wind periods averaged below 1 rad/sec, compatible with ~10-kHz-class stabilization systems. The specific fiber environment (above-ground vs. buried) has a strong impact on drift rates.

3. **Optical path length drift**: Time-of-flight variations showed strong correlation with temperature, with measured coefficients of 33.9 ps/°C (Differential Configuration) and 2.59 ns/°C (Round-Trip Configuration). The temperature at a single node can predict fiber behavior throughout the network.

Based on this characterization, the authors designed a compensation system using time-bin qubit encoding at 1350 nm, classical clock signals at 1550 nm for timing synchronization, and periodic reference pulses for polarization and frequency correction. The system achieved 97.7% fidelity (2.3% error rate) for transmitting photonic time-bin qubits from MIT-LL to Harvard across the 50-km deployed link. The protocol is designed to be compatible with silicon-vacancy (SiV) quantum memories at the receiving end.

The paper concludes that BARQNET's noise characteristics are suitable for near-term quantum networking demonstrations, including compatibility with narrow-bandwidth atomic systems, MHz-class clock rates, and integration with quantum memories. Current limitations include high loss on some fiber spans, which can be improved by replacing anomalous splices and cross-connects.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (PME) explains the quantum internet—a theorized network of interconnected quantum computers that will someday send, compute, and receive information encoded in quantum states. The quantum internet will not replace the classical internet but will coexist with it, providing new functionalities such as quantum cryptography and quantum cloud computing.

**How it works:** Quantum computers use "qubits" instead of classical bits. Unlike conventional bits (0 or 1), qubits convey information through quantum states like electron "spin," existing in a superposition of states. This allows quantum computers to solve problems like factoring large numbers, complex logistics, cryptography, and discovering new materials or drugs.

**Applications:** (1) Enhanced security through quantum key distribution (QKD) which makes encrypted messages nearly impossible to intercept. (2) Improved precision of scientific instruments for studying gravitational waves, microscopy, and electromagnetic imaging. (3) Pooled computational power across multiple quantum computers via a quantum network.

**Progress to date:**
- 2017: Chinese researchers transmitted entangled photons via satellite over 700 miles.
- April 2019: Brookhaven National Laboratory achieved entanglement over 10 miles using fiber-optic network.
- January 2020: University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory tested a 54-mile quantum loop.
- June 2022: Chicago network extended to 124 miles of optical fiber with six nodes, making it one of the longest in the nation.

**Challenges:** Qubits are easily disrupted; many require cooling to near absolute zero. Researchers are exploring defect spin qubits (e.g., in diamond or silicon carbide) that function at room temperature. Signal amplification is difficult due to the "no-clone theorem." Two transmission methods are being pursued: satellite transmission and fiber-optic cable. Researchers estimate interstate quantum networks within the US will be established in the next 10 to 15 years.

# Summary: Fireside Chat with David Awschalom on Building the Chicago Quantum Ecosystem

## Overview
This is a fireside chat (published Feb 6, 2026) between Daniel Rodan Lraine (Qblox) and Professor David Awschalom, a leading figure in quantum science and ecosystem building. Awschalom is the Liew Family Professor of Molecular Engineering at the University of Chicago, Director of the Chicago Quantum Institute, Founding Director of the Chicago Quantum Exchange (CQE), Senior Scientist at Argonne National Laboratory, and Inaugural Director of Q-NEXT (a DOE Quantum Information Science Research Center).

## Key Topics Covered

### Scientific Journey & Spintronics
- Awschalom's career began at IBM Research after his PhD at Cornell, studying how individual electrons interact with magnetic objects at the single-atom level.
- He developed time-resolved techniques to observe electron spin (a quantum mechanical property) versus charge.
- **Accidental discovery**: In a control experiment on a commercial gallium arsenide wafer, his team created spin-polarized electrons and found they remained coherent far longer than theoretical predictions. This showed that quantum coherence with spins in semiconductors could be created, controlled, transported, and detected — forming the basis for quantum information processing.

### From UCSB to Chicago
- Around 2012, University of Chicago President Bob Zimmer approached Awschalom about building a new kind of engineering program — not a traditional engineering school, but a research institute without departments focused on thematic areas.
- Awschalom proposed a quantum science and engineering program. The university invested in over a dozen new faculty positions, a new building, and a new program at a time when the field's explosive growth was not yet obvious.
- The pitch was: "blur the normal distinctions between industry, universities, and national laboratories" to build an ecosystem where information flows freely.

### The Chicago Quantum Exchange (CQE)
- Founded to literally "exchange" information and blur distinctions between academia, industry, and national labs.
- Partners include Argonne National Lab, Fermilab, Midwest universities (Illinois, Northwestern, Purdue), and international partners (Delft was the first).
- Now has nearly 70 companies and nonprofits.
- Illinois Governor Pritzker (a venture capitalist) provided significant support, helping fuel the ecosystem and attract companies to the region.

### Q-NEXT (DOE Center)
- A basic science program harnessing national lab facilities (synchrotrons, X-ray lasers, supercomputing) to develop atomic-scale quantum technologies.
- Launched a "quantum foundry" to build materials like silicon carbide, diamond, and oxide materials for quantum sensors and memories.
- Brings together a dozen universities with shared students and projects.
- Successfully renewed for another five years.

### Key Scientific Insights
- **Bottom-up vs. top-down approach**: Instead of carving devices from bulk semiconductors (top-down), Awschalom advocates for growing quantum systems from the bottom up — using molecular chemistry to design identical quantum bits atom-by-atom.
- **Hybrid platforms**: Different quantum applications will likely use different platforms (sensing, computing, communication), requiring transduction between them.
- **Key advances**: Quantum error correction improvements, expanding quantum sensors, and growing quantum networks that can entangle machines are critical for scalable quantum computing.

### Workforce Development — The Biggest Scalability Challenge
- A Boston Consulting study projected that by 2035, the Midwest US region alone will need nearly 200,000 jobs in quantum science and engineering, with global economic impact over $50 billion.
- Over 70% of these jobs will require undergraduate degrees, community college degrees, or associate degrees — not PhDs.
- Skills needed include: electrical engineering, advanced instrumentation, cryogenics, data analysis, microwave engineering, and fast electronics — with minimal quantum science knowledge required.
- Existing educational models will not suffice. Initiatives include:
  - Portable quantum programs for high school teachers and community colleges.
  - Internships for high school teachers.
  - Leveraging Illinois' third-largest community college system in the US.

### Startup Ecosystem
- Boot camp training programs for students with entrepreneurial ideas, in partnership with the Booth School of Business.
- Argonne's "Chain Reaction Innovation" program provides startup winners with lab space, salary, and access to lab resources.
- Dedicated office and lab space near campus for startups.

### Advice for Early Career Researchers
- Follow your passion — the scientific and engineering cores are portable across different quantum platforms.
- Don't fixate on a single direction; interests will evolve with learning.
- The biggest future impacts of quantum technology are likely ones we haven't imagined yet.

### On Quantum Sensing
- Molecular (including protein) qubits can be engineered to get sensors within nanometers of targets, potentially revolutionizing medicine and health sciences.
- Unlike quantum computing (where you protect qubits from the environment), sensing requires exposing qubits to the environment.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Thomas Jennewein is an Austrian physicist specializing in quantum communication and quantum key distribution. He earned his PhD under Anton Zeilinger at the University of Vienna in 2002, where he performed experiments on Bell's inequality and cryptography with entangled photons. Since 2009, he has been an associate professor at the University of Waterloo and the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC), where he leads the Quantum Photonics Laboratory. His current work focuses on satellite-based free space quantum key distribution aimed at creating a global quantum network, including the QEYSSat microsatellite mission in partnership with the Canadian Space Agency (which received $80.9M in Canadian government funding in 2017). Jennewein is also an affiliate of the Perimeter Institute, a fellow of CIFAR, and CEO and co-founder of UQDevices. Key research achievements include: co-authoring a 2015 Bell test experiment that closed both the locality and detection loopholes with a violation of seven standard deviations; observing genuine three-photon interference in 2017 (awarded a Physics World 2017 Breakthrough of the Year); and demonstrating the first quantum key distribution from a ground transmitter to a receiver on an airplane in flight (3-10 km range, generating secure keys up to 868 KB). He has received the Loschmidt-Prize (2002), an ARC Research Fellowship (2007), and the Wilhelm Exner Medal (2018).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Quantum key distribution ---
URL: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~vazirani/s05cs191/lectures/UC_Berkeley_lecture_1103.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a presentation by Richard Hughes of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) Physics Division, dated December 2, 2003, on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) as a new tool for secure communications. The presentation covers:

**Cryptography Fundamentals:** Overview of cryptography including the one-time pad (XOR encryption with a truly random key as long as the message), Kerckhoff's principles (secrecy resides in the key, not the system), and the distinction between confidentiality and authentication.

**Quantum Cryptography:** QKD enables on-demand key transfer via quantum communications, with detectability of eavesdropping ensured by laws of physics. It avoids latent vulnerability of public key broadcasts and is not vulnerable to future technology advances.

**BB84 Protocol (Bennett & Brassard, 1984):** The core QKD protocol uses conjugate coding - encoding bits in orthogonal polarization states of single photons in different bases (rectilinear and diagonal). Alice sends photons with random bits encoded in random bases; Bob measures in random bases. After transmission, they publicly compare bases and keep only bits where bases matched (sifting, ~50% efficient). Non-orthogonal polarizations cannot be faithfully distinguished or copied ("no cloning" theorem).

**Eavesdropping Detection:** Intercept-resend attacks necessarily introduce errors (e.g., 25% BER if Eve tests every bit). Alice and Bob can bound Eve's information from the observed bit error rate (BER) and remove it through privacy amplification.

**Error Correction and Privacy Amplification:** Uses bisective search ("BINARY1") for error correction, followed by privacy amplification via universal hashing to extract secret bits. The yield depends on the BER.

**Practical Implementations:**

1. **Free-space QKD (10-km range):** Demonstrated over Pajarito Mountain to LANL using 772-nm single-photon communications. Achieved ~600 Hz key rate, 45,576 secret bits/hour (day), 113,273 secret bits/45 minutes (night). Used 1-MHz sending rate with cooled Si APD detectors (η~61%).

2. **Fiber-optic QKD (48-km):** Demonstrated over 48 km of underground optical fiber using 1.3-μm pulsed lasers, single-photon interference, and cooled InGaAs APD detectors. Achieved ~98.99% visibility, ~20 Hz key rate, with ~9.3% BER.

**Security Analysis:** Addresses practical attacks including photon-number-splitting (PNS) eavesdropping and technologically feasible USD eavesdropping. Security bounds require multi-photon emission < single-photon arrival.

**Applications:** One-time pad encryption demonstrated on images. QKD enables self-sustaining key distribution from a short initial authentication key, with key replenishment through quantum communications.

**Future Directions:** Conceptual QKD LEO satellite downlinks (~106 m range, ~5 m footprint) are discussed, leveraging the atmospheric path's similarity to space transmission.
</summary>

URL: https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltechs-institute-for-quantum-information-and-matter-iqim-receives-new-6-year-grant

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Caltech's Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM) has received a $13.8 million, 6-year grant from the National Science Foundation (NSF) as part of its Physics Frontiers Centers program. First established as a Physics Frontier Center in 2011, IQIM explores quantum science topics including quantum computing, precision measurement, fundamental physics, and new quantum materials with potential applications in health care, cybersecurity, energy production, and sustainability. 

The center's roots trace back to the late 1990s when John Preskill and H.J. Jeff Kimble received DARPA funding for quantum computing research, followed by NSF funding in 2000 for the Institute for Quantum Information (IQI). IQI focused solely on theory until 2011 when NSF expanded its scope to include experimental work, transforming it into IQIM.

Looking ahead, IQIM researchers will study hardware platforms for quantum computers (including individually controlled atoms and superconducting materials), topological materials, and quantum precision measurements (metrology) leveraging entanglement. The center also runs an extensive outreach program including the Quantum Frontiers blog, short films featuring celebrities, science advising for movies, quantum games, and K-12 education programs. IQIM is led by John Preskill, with Spiros Michalakis serving as outreach manager.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Quantum research centers are springing up all over the world in recent years, but NSF recognizes that IQIM has a unique and valuable role," says John Preskill. "We've built a highly interconnected community focused on exploiting quantum technology for scientific discovery.", "I want kids to have the same intuition for quantum physics that they have about gravity," says Spiros Michalakis. "I think it's imperative to meet kids where they are at, with games and stories deeply infused with quantum science.", "In each award cycle we've refreshed IQIM by bringing in new ideas and new people who are eager to launch new collaborations. And we encourage people to try risky things. Some of our projects might fail, but you need to take a risk to make a breakthrough." - John Preskill, "All of a sudden, we attach M—matter—and it really mattered because it wasn't just that experimentalists started knocking on our door, we started to have conversations [about] how you can convert some of the theories into experiments..." - Spiros Michalakis

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 23, 2020, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) unveiled a blueprint report outlining a strategy to accelerate research in quantum science and technology, with a focus on creating a nationwide quantum Internet. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper reports on the comprehensive characterization of the Boston-Area Quantum Network (BARQNET), a 50-km fiber quantum network testbed connecting MIT Lincoln Laboratory (MIT-LL), MIT, and Harvard University. The network comprises two 42.5 km fiber spans between MIT-LL and MIT, plus two additional 7.9 km spans between MIT and Harvard, using commercial telecom fibers (some buried, some above-ground).

Key characterization results include:

1. **Optical phase/frequency noise**: Phase fluctuations were orders of magnitude larger than those on buried fibers, requiring high-bandwidth stabilization (~650 kHz). The variance of optical frequency noise per fiber span was 5.74 kHz², with strong covariance (4.88 kHz²) between co-propagating fibers, suggesting phase-stable links benefit from distributed references. The phase drifts follow a Brownian diffusion model with variance per unit length of 133 Hz²/m.

2. **Polarization drift**: Measured over multiple days, polarization drift rates correlated strongly with wind speed (power law exponent ~1.74-1.87). Mean drift rates during high-wind periods averaged below 1 rad/sec, compatible with ~10-kHz-class stabilization systems. The specific fiber environment (above-ground vs. buried) has a strong impact on drift rates.

3. **Optical path length drift**: Time-of-flight variations showed strong correlation with temperature, with measured coefficients of 33.9 ps/°C (Differential Configuration) and 2.59 ns/°C (Round-Trip Configuration). The temperature at a single node can predict fiber behavior throughout the network.

Based on this characterization, the authors designed a compensation system using time-bin qubit encoding at 1350 nm, classical clock signals at 1550 nm for timing synchronization, and periodic reference pulses for polarization and frequency correction. The system achieved 97.7% fidelity (2.3% error rate) for transmitting photonic time-bin qubits from MIT-LL to Harvard across the 50-km deployed link. The protocol is designed to be compatible with silicon-vacancy (SiV) quantum memories at the receiving end.

The paper concludes that BARQNET's noise characteristics are suitable for near-term quantum networking demonstrations, including compatibility with narrow-bandwidth atomic systems, MHz-class clock rates, and integration with quantum memories. SUMMARY:

This article from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (PME) explains the quantum internet—a theorized network of interconnected quantum computers that will someday send, compute, and receive information encoded in quantum states. The quantum internet will not replace the classical internet but will coexist with it, providing new functionalities such as quantum cryptography and quantum cloud computing.

**How it works:** Quantum computers use "qubits" instead of classical bits. Unlike conventional bits (0 or 1), qubits convey information through quantum states like electron "spin," existing in a superposition of states. This allows quantum computers to solve problems like factoring large numbers, complex logistics, cryptography, and discovering new materials or drugs.

**Applications:** (1) Enhanced security through quantum key distribution (QKD) which makes encrypted messages nearly impossible to intercept. (2) Improved precision of scientific instruments for studying gravitational waves, microscopy, and electromagnetic imaging. (3) Pooled computational power across multiple quantum computers via a quantum network.

**Progress to date:**
- 2017: Chinese researchers transmitted entangled photons via satellite over 700 miles.
- April 2019: Brookhaven National Laboratory achieved entanglement over 10 miles using fiber-optic network.
- January 2020: University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory tested a 54-mile quantum loop.
- June 2022: Chicago network extended to 124 miles of optical fiber with six nodes, making it one of the longest in the nation.

**Challenges:** Qubits are easily disrupted; many require cooling to near absolute zero. Researchers are exploring defect spin qubits (e.g., in diamond or silicon carbide) that function at room temperature. Signal amplification is difficult due to the "no-clone theorem." Two transmission methods are being pursued: satellite transmission and fiber-optic cable. Researchers estimate interstate quantum networks within the US will be established in the next 10 to 15 years.

# Canada's National Quantum Strategy

## Overview
The National Quantum Strategy (NQS) is a Government of Canada initiative to solidify Canada's position as a global leader in quantum science and technology. Canada has invested over $1 billion in quantum science between 2012 and 2022, and the strategy commits an additional $360 million over seven years (starting 2021–22). The quantum sector is projected to become a $139 billion industry in Canada with over 200,000 jobs and $42 billion in returns by 2045, potentially contributing 3% to Canada's GDP.

## Three Key Missions
1. **Quantum Computing**: Make Canada a world leader in developing, deploying and using quantum computing hardware and software. Quantum computing hardware/software could account for up to US$154 billion in global economic activity by 2030.
2. **Quantum Communications & Cybersecurity**: Ensure privacy and cyber-security through a national secure quantum communications network and post-quantum cryptography initiative.
3. **Quantum Sensing**: Enable the Government of Canada and key industries to be developers and early adopters of new quantum sensing technologies. The global market for quantum sensors is projected to be nearly US$550 million by 2026.

## Three Core Pillars
1. **Research**: Supporting basic and applied research through programs like NSERC Alliance Quantum grants, the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF - $176.3M in quantum projects), with NSERC providing over $200M and CFI over $180M since 2012.
2. **Talent**: $40 million over six years to Mitacs for internships and training, plus $5.4 million over six years to NSERC CREATE for research skills development. Emphasis on attracting, retaining and developing diverse quantum talent.
3. **Commercialization**: Supporting the growth of quantum-ready companies and technologies, with emphasis on government procurement to de-risk product development.

## Key Programs and Initiatives
- **Quantum Research and Development Initiative (QRDI)** - new program to grow government quantum capabilities
- **QEYSSat** - satellite-based quantum communications demonstration project
- **Innovative Solutions Canada (ISC)** - multiple calls for quantum computing, communications, and sensing prototypes
- **NRC Challenge Programs** - Applied Quantum Computing, High Throughput and Secure Networks, IoT Quantum Sensor Challenge

## Stakeholder Input
Consultations identified five principal quantum technologies: quantum computers, quantum software, quantum communications, quantum sensors, and quantum materials. Key areas of focus included research collaboration, talent development, commercialization support, and security concerns including post-quantum cryptography.

## Canadian Quantum Firsts
- D-Wave launched the first quantum computer (2011)
- 1Qbit recognized as first quantum software company (2015)
- Xanadu launched PennyLane, first quantum machine learning software (2018)

## Canada's Quantum Technology Landscape

This article from PostQuantum.com provides a comprehensive overview of Canada's quantum technology initiatives, covering historical context, current state, and future outlook.

**Historical Context:** Canada's engagement with quantum science began in 1984 when Canadian cryptographer Gilles Brassard co-developed the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol. Key early investments include Mike Lazaridis' $100M+ donation to establish the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) at the University of Waterloo in 2002 and the founding of D-Wave Systems in 1999, the world's first commercial quantum computing company.

**Government Initiatives:** In January 2023, Canada launched its National Quantum Strategy (NQS) with a $360M federal investment over seven years, allocating $141M for research, $45M for talent development, and $169M for commercialization. The Government of Canada has invested over $1B in quantum research since 2012.

**Academic Hubs:** Canada has three major quantum "valleys":
- Waterloo Region (Ontario): Home to IQC, Perimeter Institute, and over 250 researchers
- Vancouver (British Columbia): Stewart Blusson Quantum Matter Institute at UBC, Quantum Algorithms Institute
- Sherbrooke (Quebec): Institut Quantique and DistriQ Quantum Innovation Zone

**Private Sector:** Key companies include D-Wave (quantum annealing, 5000+ qubit systems), Xanadu (photonic quantum computing, Borealis system demonstrated quantum advantage in 2022), 1QBit, Anyon Systems, and ISARA Corp (quantum-safe cryptography).

**Quantum Communications:** Canada is developing the QEYSSat satellite (launch planned 2026) for space-based QKD, and a multi-node quantum network testbed in Quebec linking Sherbrooke, Montreal, and Quebec City.

**Quantum Sensing:** The Department of National Defence is funding quantum radar research at Waterloo's IQC ($2.7M). Other areas include quantum magnetometry (SB Quantum), quantum LIDAR, and gravimetry for Arctic surveillance and defense applications.

**Global Position:** Canada ranks among the top five countries globally in quantum research output and leads G7 nations in per-capita quantum R&D investment. Canada's strengths lie in niche leadership, talent, and international collaborations.

**Challenges:** Funding gaps, brain drain to larger tech companies, slow adoption by Canadian industry, and limited domestic market scale. The Council of Canadian Academies noted that government support has focused on R&D with "significantly less attention to stimulating technology diffusion and adoption."

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### GROUP 1: California Institute of Technology (Caltech, USA)

**Leadership Team:**
- **Jeff Kimble** (1949-2024) - William L. Valentine Professor of Physics, Emeritus. Member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, Fellow of Optica, AAAS, and APS. Received numerous awards including the Leonard Mandel Quantum Optics Award (2024), Herbert Walther Award (2013), Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize (2004), Albert A. Michelson Medal (1990), Einstein Prize for Laser Science (1989), and Optica's Max Born Award (1996). Co-founded the Institute for Quantum Information and Matter (IQIM) at Caltech and served as its inaugural director. Known for pioneering work in cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED) and the first high-fidelity demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1998, in which he teleported a beam of light (a quantum particle) across 2.7 meters. His experiments laid the foundations for quantum networks and the concept of a quantum internet. [Source: Caltech Mourns Kimble, UTPhysicsHistorySite]
- **John Preskill** - Professor of Theoretical Physics at Caltech, Director of IQIM. Leads the center's theoretical quantum information research. Teaches Ph/CS 219: Quantum Computation covering quantum information theory, quantum algorithms, quantum error correction, quantum Shannon theory, quantum cryptography, teleportation, and fault-tolerant quantum computation. [Source: IQIM, Caltech IQIM Grant Announcement]
- **Oskar Painter** - Professor of Applied Physics at Caltech. Teaches APh 150: Introduction to Quantum Devices covering quantum technologies for processing and communicating quantum information including qubits, quantum gates, quantum-limited measurement, atomic quantum optical memories, optomechanics, color centers, superconducting quantum circuits, and quantum plasmonics. [Source: IQIM Classes]

**Key Publications & Venues:**
- First high-fidelity demonstration of quantum teleportation (1998) - a landmark experiment that laid the foundations for quantum networks [Source: UTPhysicsHistorySite, Caltech Mourns Kimble]
- IQIM researchers publish in Nature, Science, Physical Review Letters, PRX Quantum, and other top venues [Source: IQIM, Caltech IQIM Grant]

**Funding Sources:**

- **NSF**: Funding in 2000 for the Institute for Quantum Information (IQI), which focused solely on theory until 2011 when it became IQIM [Source: Caltech IQIM Grant Announcement]
- **DOE**: Caltech is a central partner in four of the five DOE National QIS Research Centers receiving $625 million renewal funding. Caltech is named as a partner in Q-NEXT. [Source: Caltech LinkedIn, Q-NEXT Renewal Announcement]

**Major Projects:**
- **IQIM (Institute for Quantum Information and Matter)**: NSF Physics Frontiers Center exploring quantum science topics including quantum computing, precision measurement, fundamental physics, and new quantum materials. Research programs span quantum information physics, next-generation quantum metrology, and building and driving quantum matter. [Source: IQIM, Caltech IQIM Grant]

**Technology Approach:**

- **AFOSR Quantum Memories MURI**: Dirk Englund is a team member [Source: Kuzmich Research Group Team Page]

### GROUP 3: Harvard University (USA)

**Leadership Team:**

Pioneer in quantum optics, NV center physics, cavity QED with nanophotonic systems, long-range entanglement of NV centers. Started quantum network research nearly 25 years ago. **Key Publications & Venues:**
- "Entanglement of nanophotonic quantum memory nodes in a telecom network" (2024, Nature) - demonstration of two-node quantum network using SiV centers in nanophotonic diamond cavities integrated with telecom fiber network. Key achievements: remote entanglement of electron spins between two spatially separated SiV centers with success rates up to 1 Hz; remote entanglement of long-lived nuclear spins (²⁹Si nuclei) with storage times exceeding 1 second; entanglement distribution through telecom fiber networks using bidirectional quantum frequency conversion (QFC) from 737 nm to 1350 nm (telecom O-band); entanglement through up to 40 km spools of low-loss telecom fiber and a 35-km deployed fiber loop in the Boston area urban environment (17 dB loss, crossing four municipalities). System parameters: single-photon cooperativity of 12.4 (node A) and 1.5 (node B); electron spin coherence times of 125 μs and 134 μs; QFC efficiency of 5.4%; Bell-state fidelities of 0.86(3) for electron-electron entanglement and 0.77(5) for nuclear-nuclear entanglement with error detection. [Source: Nature 2024]
- Harvard physicists demonstrated the world's first metro-area quantum computer network in Boston, published in Nature (May 2024). Successfully entangled two quantum memory nodes separated by a roughly 22-mile loop of existing Boston-area telecommunication fiber, passing through Cambridge, Somerville, Watertown, and Boston. The two nodes were located a floor apart in Harvard's Laboratory for Integrated Science and Engineering. Each node is a tiny quantum computer made from a diamond sliver with a silicon-vacancy center defect, containing two qubits: an electron spin for communication and a nuclear spin for memory. [Source: Harvard Gazette]
- "Telecom Networking with a Diamond Quantum Memory" (2024, PRX Quantum) - demonstrated low-noise, bidirectional quantum frequency conversion enabling a solid-state quantum memory (SiV center in diamond) to directly interface with telecom-band systems. Converted visible-band single photons from SiV centers to the telecom O band while maintaining low noise (g²(0) < 0.1) and high indistinguishability (V = 89 ± 8%). Converted telecom-band time-bin pulses sent across a lossy and noisy 50-km deployed fiber link (connecting MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Harvard University in the Boston area) to the visible band and entangling them with a diamond quantum memory with fidelity ≥ 87 ± 2.5%. [Source: PRX Quantum]
