### ADDITIONAL CROSS-CUTTING INFORMATION

**Major DOE Quantum Internet Blueprint:**
- On July 23, 2020, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) unveiled a blueprint report outlining a strategy to accelerate research in quantum science and technology, with a focus on creating a nationwide quantum Internet. The blueprint emerged from the Quantum Internet Blueprint Workshop, co-chaired by ESnet Director Inder Monga, which identified four priority research opportunities: providing foundational building blocks for a quantum Internet, integrating multiple quantum networking devices, creating repeating/switching/routing for quantum entanglement, and enabling error correction. Five key milestones were established: verifying secure quantum protocols over fiber networks, inter-campus/intra-city entanglement distribution, intercity quantum communication using entanglement swapping, interstate quantum entanglement distribution using quantum repeaters, and building a multi-institutional ecosystem for operational infrastructure. DOE's 17 National Laboratories will serve as the backbone. [Source: ESnet News]

**DOE $625 Million Quantum Centers Renewal:**
- The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced $625 million in funding to renew its five National Quantum Information Science (QIS) Research Centers, originally established under the 2018 National Quantum Initiative Act. The announcement was made by DOE Under Secretary of Science Darío Gil during keynote remarks at the Chicago Quantum Summit. The five renewed centers include: C2QA (Brookhaven), SQMS (Fermilab), Q-NEXT (Argonne), QSA (Lawrence Berkeley), and QSC (Oak Ridge). Each center will receive $125 million over five years, with $125 million in Fiscal Year 2025 dollars. [Source: Chicago Quantum Exchange]
- DOE Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil challenged the QIS community to "demonstrate a new scientific instrument for the Nation by 2028: the first generation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer designed to accelerate scientific discovery." [Source: Caltech LinkedIn]

**DOE $24 Million for Quantum Networks:**
- DOE announced $24 million for three collaborative projects in quantum network research, supporting scalable quantum network communications. Selected by competitive peer review under the DOE National Laboratory Announcement "Scientific Enablers of Scalable Quantum Communications." [Source: DOE]

**National Quantum Initiative Act (2018):**
- Chris Monroe played instrumental role in crafting the 2018 National Quantum Initiative Act [Source: Christopher Monroe Wikipedia]
- Federal investment in QIS is approximately $200 million/year across DOD (AFOSR, ARO, ONR, DARPA), DOE, IARPA, NIST, and NSF [Source: 2016 NSTC Report]

**Center for Quantum Networks (CQN):**
- NSF Engineering Research Center founded in 2020 by Prof. Saikat Guha at University of Arizona, now headquartered at UArizona with Prof. Guha at UMD as co-Director. Core partner universities include MIT, UMD, UMass Amherst, and Harvard University. Focuses on developing the full technology stack to upgrade the internet to carry quantum data globally, including building the first viable and scalable quantum repeater. Research spans three thrusts: (1) spin-based memories and color center qubit fabrication, (2) error correction, entanglement distillation, and quantum repeater architecture, and (3) quantum networking architectures, algorithms, and protocols. Operates multiple testbeds: BARQNET (Boston area), QUCSON (Tucson area), MARQI (UMD campus), and a Virtual Testbed digital twin. [Source: CQN Description]

**AFOSR Quantum Memories MURI:**
- Collaborative team including Alex Kuzmich (UMich, Group Leader), Brian Kennedy (Georgia Tech), Dirk Englund (Columbia/MIT), Vladan Vuletic (MIT), Thad Walker (Wisconsin), Mark Saffman (Wisconsin), Marko Loncar (Harvard), Mikhail Lukin (Harvard), Jelena Vuckovic (Stanford), and Luming Duan (UMich). [Source: Kuzmich Research Group Team Page]

**Diamond Integrated Quantum Photonics (Roadmap):**
- Key findings from roadmap paper (Journal of Physics: Photonics, 2021): NV centers have demonstrated loophole-free photon-mediated entanglement between distant spins, deterministic entanglement delivery exceeding decoherence rates, spin coherence over one second, and a 10-qubit quantum register with entanglement of 7 qubits. SiV centers have shown superior optical properties including charge and spectral stability in nanophotonic cavities, enabling an integrated single-photon switch, coherent interaction of two SiV spins via cavity modes, and memory-enhanced photonic Bell-state measurements. Cooperativity of spin-photon interfaces exceeds 100, and over 90% of SiV photons can be extracted into optical fibers. Challenges: NV centers have only 4% emission into the zero-phonon line (ZPL), limiting entanglement rates (currently 39 Hz max). [Source: DTIC Diamond Roadmap]

**Quantum Memories Review:**
- Quantum memories are at the heart of photonic quantum technologies. Three categories of protocols: (1) Optically controlled memories (EIT and Raman-based), (2) Engineered absorption memories (GEM and AFC), and (3) Hybrid schemes. Physical systems: rare-earth ion-doped solids (spin storage coherence times up to 370±60 minutes in ¹⁵¹Eu³⁺:Y₂SiO₅), NV centers in diamond, Raman scattering in solids, alkali vapours. [Source: Journal of Modern Optics 2016]

**PRX Quantum 2024 - Atom-Photon Entanglement over 101 km:**
- Researchers from LMU München demonstrated entanglement between a single ⁸⁷Rb atom and a single photon transmitted through 101 km of telecom fiber with fidelity of 70.8 ± 2.4%. Coherence time of the single atom prolonged to 10 ms. Wavelength converted to telecom S-band via polarization-preserving quantum frequency conversion. A coherence time of 7 ms effectively would allow entanglement distribution over fiber links of almost 1000 km. [Source: PRX Quantum 2024]

Pan Jianwei (born 11 March 1970, Dongyang, Zhejiang, China) is a Chinese quantum physicist and academic administrator. He is a professor and Executive Vice President of the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), and Vice Chairman of the Jiusan Society. He earned his bachelor's and master's degrees from USTC and his PhD from the University of Vienna under Nobel laureate Anton Zeilinger.

Pan is known for groundbreaking work in quantum entanglement, quantum information, and quantum computers. His team demonstrated five-photon entanglement in 2004. In August 2016, under his leadership, the world's first quantum satellite (Micius) launched as part of the Quantum Experiments at Space Scale project. In 2017, his team demonstrated entanglement distribution over 1200 km using the satellite. In 2021, his teams built two quantum computers: Zuchongzhi 2.1 (superconducting circuits), claimed to be one million times faster than Google's Sycamore, and Jiuzhang (using photons).

He was elected to the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2011 (age 41, one of the youngest), and to the World Academy of Sciences in 2012. In 2017, Nature named him one of Nature's 10, labeling him "Father of Quantum." He received the Future Science Prize (2017), was named in Time's 100 Most Influential People (2018), received the R.W. Wood Prize (2019), ZEISS Research Award (2020), and the IEEE Photonics Society Quantum Electronics Award (2026). In July 2026, UNESCO awarded him the UNESCO-Russia Mendeleev International Prize in the Basic Sciences for his work on the Micius satellite enabling quantum key distribution and teleportation over thousands of kilometers. He was elected a Foreign Fellow of the Royal Society in 2024.

<summary>
# Quantum Information Processing with Photons and Atoms - Jian Wei Pan (USTC, China)

## Overview
This is a recorded MCQST Colloquium talk from May 28, 2025, by Prof. Jian-Wei Pan of the University of Science and Technology of China (USTC). Pan is a leading figure in quantum information science, known for pioneering multi-particle interferometry, quantum experiments in space (Micius satellite), and demonstrating quantum computational advantage.

## Key Topics Covered

### Quantum Communication Challenges
1. **Security loopholes** from imperfect single-photon sources and detectors - solved via decoy-state QKD (2005) and measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD
2. **Photon loss in fiber** - exponential loss limits distance; e.g., only 0.3 photons transmitted on average over 1,000 km fiber even with perfect sources/detectors

### Quantum Repeaters
- Based on entanglement swapping and purification
- Pan's group demonstrated first entanglement swapping (1998), high-precision swapping (2003), and entanglement purification with linear optics (2003)
- Quantum memory lifetime improved by 8 orders of magnitude from 2008 to 2016
- Recent achievement: first multi-node entanglement-based quantum network over a metropolitan area
- Target: deterministic entanglement distribution over 1,000 km in 4-5 years

### Satellite-Based Quantum Communication
- Micius satellite launched in 2016 (first quantum satellite)
- Achieved QKD at 1,000 km scale with key rate ~1 kHz (20 orders of magnitude higher transmission efficiency than fiber)
- Intercontinental QKD demonstrated (Beijing-Vienna, 2018)
- Future plans: 4 micro-satellite constellation (2026), GEO satellite (2027) for entanglement distribution over 10,000 km
- Proposed quantum-enhanced telescope arrays and ultra-precise optical clocks (10^-19 stability)

### Quantum Computational Advantage
- **Superconducting approach**: Zuchongzhi #2 (66 qubits, 2021), Zuchongzhi #3 (105 qubits) - advantage ratio improved by 6 orders of magnitude over Google's Sycamore
- **Photonic approach**: Gaussian boson sampling with 76 photons (2020), 3,000 photons in latest experiment - projected advantage ratio ~40 orders of magnitude
- Important distinction: original Google 2019 claim of 10,000 years was overturned to 14 seconds by classical algorithms

### Quantum Simulation
- **Fractional quantum Hall effect**: demonstrated with superconducting resonators (4×4 array of "plasmonium" boxes), observing quantized Hall conductivity at 1/2
- **Ultracold Fermi gases**: 
  - Observed first and second sound in unitary Fermi superfluids, extracted transport coefficients near quantum limit
  - Demonstrated pseudogap in unitary Fermi gas above transition temperature (smoking gun evidence)
  - First experimental verification of antiferromagnetic phase transition in Fermi-Hubbard model (with ~800,000 lattice sites)

### Platform Comparison (Pan's Perspective)
- **Superconducting qubits**: Most advanced currently (few hundred functional qubits), but cooling power limits scaling to millions
- **Neutral atoms**: Promising but requires high-power laser systems not yet commercially available
- **Photons**: Best long-term candidate if deterministic CNOT operation can be achieved; loss correction codes are simpler than error correction; main challenge is achieving strong coupling between individual photons

### Future Outlook
- Global quantum network combining metropolitan fiber networks, quantum repeaters, and satellite constellations
- Universal quantum computation with millions of qubits expected in 10-15+ years
- Near-term (5 years): coherent manipulation of hundreds to thousands of qubits for investigating high-Tc superconductivity and quantum Hall effects
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), dated May 13, 2021, argues that the world is on the precipice of a "quantum revolution" and that Australia needs a clear strategy, political leadership, and organized investment to avoid being left behind. The report notes that while Australia benefited from the digital revolution, it missed its opportunity to play a major role in computing and communications, and should not repeat that mistake with quantum technologies.

**Key Problem:** The pace of global quantum technology investment accelerated rapidly between 2015 and 2020, and Australia is falling behind. Before 2015, Australia ranked sixth in sovereign investment among nine major economies; today it ranks last. Investment by China, the US, France, Germany, the EU, India, and Russia now exceeds Australian investment by a factor of 10-100. China has flagged over A$13 billion for a quantum center, Germany announced A$3.15 billion, France announced A$2.85 billion, and the Netherlands announced A$960 million. Australia maintains a strong position in quantum talent but is losing researchers overseas (a "talent leak").

**Key Recommendations:**
1. The Prime Minister should appoint a dedicated minister for critical and emerging technologies.
2. The government should lay groundwork for a post-COVID A$15 billion technology stimulus, including A$3-4 billion for quantum technologies.
3. Develop a national technology strategy with quantum as a key part, and expand the Critical Technologies Policy Coordination Office into a "National Coordinator for Technology."
4. Lead a "National Quantum Initiative" forming an "Australian Distributed Quantum Zone" — a collaboration of universities, corporations, and start-ups.
5. Expand education and training programs nationwide to build quantum literacy, and attract back talent that has moved offshore.

**Quantum Technology Applications:** The report covers three main pillars of quantum technology:
- **Quantum Computing** (15+ years for a computer capable of cracking public-key cryptosystems) — will affect materials science, logistics, and cryptography.

- **Quantum Sensing** — includes magnetometry (undersea detection), atomic clocks (GPS/timing), and gravitometry (detecting underground structures/mineral deposits).

**Geopolitical Implications:** The report outlines scenarios where quantum technology could affect relations between Western allies and China, tip the balance between regional powers, and disrupt digital economies (including threats to cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin).

**Australia's Current Position:** Australia has a long history of leadership in quantum technology dating back to the 1990s, with ARC Centres of Excellence (CQC2T, EQUS) and emerging start-ups (Q-CTRL, Quintessence Labs, Silicon Quantum Computing). --- SOURCE 4: Advancements in superconducting quantum computing ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12285583

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive review article titled "Advancements in superconducting quantum computing" published in the National Science Review (2025) by Jiang, Deng, Fan, et al. It provides an overview of superconducting quantum computing (SQC) development, including:

**Historical Development:** SQC began with the first superconducting qubit realized by Nakamura et al. in 1999. Key milestones include the transmon qubit proposal (2007), the Xmon variant (2013), and achieving single-qubit gate fidelities of 99.94% and two-qubit gate fidelities of 99.4% in 2014, surpassing the surface code error-correction threshold.

**Fabrication:** SC quantum chips leverage semiconductor fabrication techniques. Coherence times have increased from nanoseconds to milliseconds over 20+ years. Key materials include aluminum (Al), niobium (Nb), and tantalum (Ta). Multi-layer wiring via flip-chip bonding and through-silicon vias (TSV) enables scalability. Josephson junctions (Al/AlOx/Al) are fabricated using shadow evaporation or planar overlap techniques.

**Gate Operations:** Single-qubit gates use resonant microwave pulses with DRAG techniques to mitigate leakage. Two-qubit gates are categorized by architecture (fixed-frequency, tunable, tunable coupling) and include CR gates, CZ gates, iSWAP gates, and parametric gates. Many groups achieve gate errors below 1%, with some under 0.1%.

**Recent Experimental Progress:**
- Multi-qubit entangled states: GHZ states have been prepared up to 60 qubits (ZJU, 2024).
- Quantum advantage: Six landmark random circuit sampling (RCS) experiments from Google and USTC (2019-2024), with the latest using 83 qubits and 32 circuit depth.
- Quantum error correction: Surface codes have been demonstrated with various code distances. Google's 2024 results showed logical qubit error rates below physical qubit error rates (break-even point). Quantum LDPC codes are being explored for higher efficiency.
- Error mitigation: IBM (2023) demonstrated zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) on a 127-qubit chip with 60-layer depth. Probabilistic error cancelation (PEC) and symmetry-based error mitigation are also discussed.

**Alternative Qubit Systems:** The review mentions boson-encoded qubits (cat codes, binomial codes, GKP codes), fluxonium qubits, and qudits as alternative approaches.

**Challenges:** Scaling SQC faces challenges including crosstalk, fabrication variability, hardware imperfections, and the large qubit overhead required for surface codes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: SNU–University of Seoul Joint Research Team Develops Programmable Photonic Integrated Circuit That Slows Light on Demand - Research Highlights - Research Highlights - Research - Seoul National University ---
URL: https://en.snu.ac.kr/research/highlights?md=v&bbsidx=173072

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A joint research team from Seoul National University (SNU) and the University of Seoul has developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light on demand, published on June 30 in the journal Advanced Science. The team, led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu (SNU Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering) and Professor Xianji Piao (University of Seoul), addressed the fundamental challenge that light travels at a fixed speed, which has limited optical computing applications.

The researchers devised a method to control both the speed and shape of optical signals using a programmable photonic integrated circuit based on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT). Unlike conventional CRIT structures with fixed operational characteristics, the new design treats two optical states (bright mode and dark mode) as a single unified degree of freedom and introduces two controllable loop couplers, enabling reconfigurable resonator structures.

Key achievements include:
- Demonstrated control of "slow light" with higher freedom than any previously proposed method
- Theoretically proved ability to control bandwidth, passband shape, delay, and transmission characteristics
- Demonstrated through 3D electromagnetic simulations that the device can be implemented on a silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) photonic integrated circuit platform
- Verified reliable operation when accounting for real-world factors like material losses, thermal crosstalk, and fabrication variations

The technology enables a single optical chip to perform multiple functions (signal synchronization, variable delay lines, optical buffers, frequency conversion), potentially reducing power consumption in data centers and AI servers while improving data processing efficiency. The research was supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center program, Basic Research Laboratory program, and Young Researcher Program.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Physical Review Applied on April 9, 2024, by Yi-Kai Liu and Dustin Moody of NIST, reviews the current status of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and explores how quantum technologies can further enhance cybersecurity beyond what PQC alone can provide.

**Key Points:**

1. **Post-Quantum Cryptography Status**: NIST has selected several schemes for public-key encryption and digital signatures to become US government standards, marking the beginning of a major transition in Internet security. These schemes are designed to resist attacks from quantum computers using Shor's algorithm and Grover's algorithm, which threaten current cryptosystems like RSA and elliptic curve cryptography.

2. **Limitations of PQC**: PQC does not address all cybersecurity problems. Outstanding issues include software/hardware imperfections that leak secret key information (side-channel attacks), and the challenge of securely handling secret keys including their generation, storage, backup, and transport.

3. **Quantum Technologies for Protecting Secret Keys**: The authors propose using quantum phenomena like uncloneability (from the no-cloning theorem) and self-testing/verification of quantum devices to construct secure hardware. Key techniques include:
   - **Device-independent random number generators (RNGs)** using Bell tests, which can certify true randomness.
   - **Quantum uncloneable functionalities** like quantum money, one-time signatures, and one-time programs using single-qubit quantum memories.
   - **Incremental upgrades to HSMs** starting with QKD systems, then moving to Bell-test-based RNGs, and eventually implementing uncloneable cryptographic functions.

4. **Trustworthy Quantum Computations**: The authors discuss verifying quantum computations, particularly for analog quantum simulators and random sampling experiments. They propose "trapdoor Hamiltonians" as a potential verification method. They also discuss protecting quantum data (quantum states) for use as scientific reference materials.

5. **Practical Roadmap**: A hybrid approach is suggested where low-cost HSMs with QKD hardware could be deployed now, and later upgraded to perform device-independent RNG using more expensive matter-qubit HSMs, analogous to the public key infrastructure's hierarchical certificate authority model.
</summary>

This is a 2019 European Commission Joint Research Centre technical report surveying worldwide quantum key distribution (QKD) in-field deployments. It covers both terrestrial and satellite-based QKD networks, focusing on technology demonstrated at kilometre scale over days or longer. 

**Asia:**
- **China:** Has the largest network — a 2,000 km Beijing-Shanghai backbone with 32 trusted nodes, operating at ~20-30 kbps secure key rate. Metropolitan networks in Beijing, Shanghai, Hefei (46 nodes), and Jinan (56 nodes). The Micius satellite (launched Aug 2016) enables satellite-to-ground QKD (~1.1 kbps), intercontinental QKD with Europe, and entanglement distribution over 1,200 km. Both discrete-variable (DV-QKD) and continuous-variable (CV-QKD) systems deployed. Commercial vendors include QuantumCTek, China Quantum Technologies, and Anhui Qasky.
- **Japan:** Tokyo QKD Network (6 nodes, commercial fibres) tested multiple protocols. Demonstrations include video OTP encryption at 128 kbps, sustained 300 kbps over 34 days (Toshiba), and CV-QKD co-existing with 18 Tbps classical traffic. SOTA microsatellite demonstrated QKD-enabling QBER from LEO in 2016.
- **South Korea:** Government-funded ~250 km quantum backbone. SK Telecom deployed QKD achieving 10 kbps over 50 km, feeding AES-256 encryptors at 120 Gbps total. Acquired controlling stake in ID Quantique (2018) and collaborating with Nokia and Deutsche Telekom.

**Europe:**
- **Austria:** SECOQC project (2008) in Vienna — landmark 6-system interoperability demonstration over 3 days, with links up to 83 km.
- **Switzerland:** SwissQuantum (March 2009–Jan 2011) — first long-term continuous QKD network (3 nodes, dark fibre), operating three functional layers.
- **Italy:** Italian Quantum Backbone (~1,860 km fibre, Turin to Matera). QKD tested on 100 km link (0.25 kbps) and 40 km Florence link (3.4 kbps). Plans for Sicily-Malta undersea link. Satellite experiments using Matera ground station.
- **Spain:** Madrid Quantum Network focusing on QKD integration with SDN and telecom networks. Testing CV-QKD with Huawei, co-existing with 2 Tbps classical traffic.
- **UK:** Networks in Cambridge, Bristol, and Cambridge-to-London link. Toshiba's multiplexed high-speed QKD demonstrated. 5G network integration with SDN in Bristol.
- **Russia:** Test networks in Moscow (banking applications) and St Petersburg (high-speed protocol testing).
- **Poland:** Well-developed plans for network in Wrocław area.

**North America:**
- **USA:** Early experiments in Boston (2004). Batelle deployed in Ohio (2013). Quantum Xchange (2019) linking New York to New Jersey data centres, with plans for Boston-Washington link. NASA published quantum roadmap for space activities.
- **Canada:** Ground deployments in Calgary. Satellite mission preparations underway, building on 2016 quantum uplink to aircraft demonstration.

**Africa:**
- **South Africa:** 4-node test network in Durban (2009), longest link 27 km, using commercial equipment in dark fibre.

**Technical Summary:** Most deployments use BB84 and related single-photon protocols, but coherent one-way and CV-QKD also deployed at scale. Quantum channels typically in dark fibre, though multiplexed quantum-classical channels demonstrated. Entanglement-based QKD at lower technology readiness. Key rate depends on distance, protocol, hardware, fibre type, and system configuration.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: SNU–University of Seoul joint research team develops ... ---
URL: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1136567

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A joint research team led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of Seoul National University (SNU), in collaboration with Professor Xianji Piao of the University of Seoul, has developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light on demand. The research addresses the limitations of conventional electronic semiconductors in AI and data processing by enabling optical computing with low-power, ultra-fast processing capabilities.

The team devised a method to control both the speed and shape of optical signals using coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT) structures. By treating two optical states (bright mode and dark mode) as a unified design parameter and introducing two controllable loop couplers, they created reconfigurable photonic circuits that can delay and control light propagation—overcoming the traditional limitation of fixed operational characteristics after fabrication.

The study was published on June 30, 2026 in *Advanced Science*. Through numerical simulations and 3D electromagnetic simulations, the team demonstrated real-time dynamic adjustment of optical pulse propagation speed, delay control, and frequency conversion—all achievable on a silicon nitride (Si₃N₄) photonic integrated circuit platform. They also verified the design's reliability against fabrication-related factors such as material losses, thermal crosstalk, and coupling fluctuations.

This technology is expected to enable single-chip optical processing with multiple functions—including signal synchronization, variable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion—potentially reducing power consumption in data centers and AI servers while improving processing efficiency. The researchers plan to expand toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.", Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.", The study was published on June 30 in the renowned international journal Advanced Science., The research was supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

URL: https://link.aps.org/accepted/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.21.040501

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Physical Review Applied on April 9, 2024, by Yi-Kai Liu and Dustin Moody of NIST, reviews the current status of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and explores how quantum technologies can further enhance cybersecurity beyond what PQC alone can provide.

**Key Points:**

1. **Post-Quantum Cryptography Status**: NIST has selected several schemes for public-key encryption and digital signatures to become US government standards, marking the beginning of a major transition in Internet security. These schemes are designed to resist attacks from quantum computers using Shor's algorithm and Grover's algorithm, which threaten current cryptosystems like RSA and elliptic curve cryptography.

2. **Limitations of PQC**: PQC does not address all cybersecurity problems. Outstanding issues include software/hardware imperfections that leak secret key information (side-channel attacks), and the challenge of securely handling secret keys including their generation, storage, backup, and transport.

3. **Quantum Technologies for Protecting Secret Keys**: The authors propose using quantum phenomena like uncloneability (from the no-cloning theorem) and self-testing/verification of quantum devices to construct secure hardware. Key techniques include:
   - **Device-independent random number generators (RNGs)** using Bell tests, which can certify true randomness.
   - **Quantum uncloneable functionalities** like quantum money, one-time signatures, and one-time programs using single-qubit quantum memories.
   - **Incremental upgrades to HSMs** starting with QKD systems, then moving to Bell-test-based RNGs, and eventually implementing uncloneable cryptographic functions.

4. **Trustworthy Quantum Computations**: The authors discuss verifying quantum computations, particularly for analog quantum simulators and random sampling experiments. They propose "trapdoor Hamiltonians" as a potential verification method. They also discuss protecting quantum data (quantum states) for use as scientific reference materials.

5. **Practical Roadmap**: A hybrid approach is suggested where low-cost HSMs with QKD hardware could be deployed now, and later upgraded to perform device-independent RNG using more expensive matter-qubit HSMs, analogous to the public key infrastructure's hierarchical certificate authority model.
</summary>

The backbone network features 145 fiber backbone nodes and 144 fiber links (total ~10,103 km), with average inter-node distance of ~70 km and average attenuation of 18.61 dB per link. Of the 145 backbone nodes, 41 are backbone access nodes with metropolitan network access capabilities. Metropolitan networks have been deployed in 20 cities, comprising 36 access nodes supporting more than 800 user nodes.

The network architecture follows ITU-T Y.3802 and comprises five layers: quantum layer, key management layer, QKD network control layer, QKD network management layer, and application layer. The control layer uses a hierarchical architecture with Level-1 and Level-2 controllers.

Seven types of QKD devices are deployed: four high-speed systems (Types I-IV) in backbone networks based on the decoy-state BB84 protocol, and three metropolitan systems (Types V-VII) including both discrete-variable and continuous-variable (CV-QKD) approaches. The backbone systems operate at 625 MHz (Types I-III) or 312.5 MHz (Type IV). Security countermeasures are implemented against photon-number-splitting attacks, Trojan-horse attacks, laser seeding attacks, time-shift attacks, and detector blinding attacks.

Long-term performance evaluation over a 10-week period on the Harbin-Shenzhen backbone path (64 KM-Links) showed minimum secure key rate of 9.75 kbps and maximum of 359.89 kbps. The network demonstrated consistent secure key rates throughout extended operation, and ring-topology protection was found to be particularly necessary for resilience against disruptions.

The paper concludes that CN-QCN will become an important information security infrastructure in China, and can serve as a testbed for future quantum internet technologies including quantum measurement and quantum relay.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IEEE Spectrum article reports on China's nearly complete 2,000-kilometer quantum key distribution (QKD) fiber-optic link between Beijing and Shanghai, expected to be finished by the end of 2016 (the article's publication date). The backbone will connect quantum networks in four cities and is complemented by a quantum science satellite launched in August 2016. Led by physicist Jian-Wei Pan from the University of Science and Technology of China, the project uses 32 "trusted nodes" as relays approximately every 100 km to refresh the quantum signal, since photons carrying quantum keys cannot travel indefinitely without being absorbed or scattered. While trusted nodes introduce a security vulnerability (eavesdropping is possible at those 32 physical locations), the approach is still considered more secure than traditional communications where eavesdropping is possible at any point. The article notes that quantum repeaters using entanglement could eliminate the need for trusted nodes but remain in early development. QKD is described as "in principle, unhackable" because any eavesdropping attempt creates detectable errors. The piece also discusses QKD as one approach to countering future quantum computers that could break current public-key cryptography, alongside "post-quantum" algorithmic alternatives.

args.summary:
This is the faculty profile page for Dr. Yingying Peng (彭莹莹) at the International Center for Quantum Materials (ICQM), Peking University. Dr. Peng is an Assistant Professor whose research focuses on using resonant/non-resonant inelastic, elastic, and time-resolved X-ray scattering methods to study elementary collective phenomena in condensed matter, including high-temperature superconductors, electron correlations, spin/charge ordering, and quantum criticality.

**Education:**
- Ph.D. (2008-2013) in Condensed Matter Physics, Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
- B.S. (2004-2008) in Physics, Wuhan University

**Professional Appointments:**
- 2019-present: Assistant Professor, ICQM, Peking University
- 2018-2019: Postdoctoral Research Associate, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
- 2013-2017: Postdoctoral Fellow, Politecnico di Milano, Italy

**Key Publications (selected from 26 listed):**
- Research on d-wave superconducting gap in high-Tc cuprates via RIXS (Phys. Rev. B, 2026)
- Photoinduced dynamics and chiral charge density waves in 1T-TiSe2 (Phys. Rev. Lett., 2025)
- Using magnetic dynamics to measure spin gap in a Kitaev material (npj Quantum Materials, 2025)
- Observation of circular dichroism induced by electronic chirality (Phys. Rev. Lett., 2024, Editors' Suggestion)
- Evolution from charge-ordered insulator to high-Tc superconductor in Bi2Sr2(Ca,Dy)Cu2O8+δ (Nature Communications, 2024)
- Prevailing charge order in overdoped cuprates beyond the superconducting dome (Phys. Rev. Lett., 2023, Editors' Suggestion)
- Coexistence of multiple stacking charge density waves in Kagome superconductor CsV3Sb5 (Phys. Rev. Research, 2023)
- Paramagnons and high-temperature superconductivity in mercury-based cuprates (Nature Communications, 2022)
- Re-entrant charge order in overdoped (Bi,Pb)2.12Sr1.88CuO6+δ (Nature Materials, 2018)
- Influence of apical oxygen on in-plane exchange interaction in cuprate superconductors (Nature Physics, 2017)
- Disappearance of nodal gap across insulator-superconductor transition (Nature Communications, 2013)

**Open Positions:** Dr. Peng's group plans to recruit 1-2 graduate students per year, seeking candidates with strong physics background, good communication skills, and willingness to travel for experiments.

Shawn Walker John McVeigh John Bell Linda Deravin Glen Coleman Cliff Kaye Patrick Lay Geoff Pryde Andrew White Stuart Blackwell Gudrun Seynsche Grant Woollett Peter Schubel Guy Barry Michael Harvey Mark Jacobs Prasad KDV Yarlagadda OAM** Tom Stace liked this [View Post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/robert-sang-aa41377_we-have-formally-opened-our-quantum-cyrogenic-activity-7453237568340643840-RxRj) ![Activity Image](https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D5622AQERFqIRaf0boQ/feedshare-shrink_800/B56Z284ED6GgAc-/0/1776990307168?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=rkq4wuD9LG86lMZchfVI-AA71-UyC97OqUIy9AXf91I) - **How do you move to support a future state where agents will buy on behalf of consumers? args.summary:
Tom Stace is a theoretical quantum physicist and quantum engineer based in the Greater Brisbane Area, Australia. He is the co-founder and CEO of Analog Quantum Circuits (AQC), a company specializing in superconducting quantum circuits. He holds a PhD from the University of Cambridge (2000-2003). 

Key professional activities and affiliations include:
- AQC is actively hiring a Quantum Hardware / Microwave Engineer for their South-East Queensland team.
- AQC partnered with the University of Southern Queensland to open the Quantum Cryogenic Facility (QC Labs) at the Springfield campus — the first commercial facility of its kind in Australia, funded by the Queensland Government's Quantum and Advanced Technologies Commercialisation Infrastructure Program.
- AQC is collaborating with Dr. Maja Cassidy and her team at UNSW to accelerate R&D in cryogenic microwave devices.
- Stace works closely with Kavan Modi and Gavin Brennen at Monash University on quantum computing, quantum information, and complex quantum processes.
- He was part of a CSIRO quantum panel discussing how to apply quantum technology to business.
- Postdoc positions in quantum computing and quantum information are available at Monash University in collaboration with Stace and Gavin Brennen.
- Stace has 500+ connections and 1312 followers on LinkedIn.
- His activity reflects engagement with major quantum computing developments, including Q-CTRL's Fermionic simulation results on IBM hardware (120 qubits, 9,000+ 2-qubit gates, achieving 3,000x speedup) and heterogeneous architecture research showing a 138× reduction in physical qubit requirements for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

# Professor Ping Koy Lam

![Lam, Ping Koy profile](/contact/people/image.php/294/440/1/image.webp)

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Position | Departmental Visitor |
| Department | [Quantum Science & Technology](/research/qst) |

| Office phone | [(02) 612 58378](tel:+61261258378) |
| Email | [Ping.Lam@anu.edu.au](mailto:Ping.Lam@anu.edu.au) |
| Office | Physics New 2 41 |

* [About](?ID=294 "About")

## Research interests

Quantum Optics, Quantum Information, Atom-Light Interaction, Quantum Metrology, Nonlinear Optics

## Biography

Ping Koy Lam completed his degree with a double major in Mathematics and Physics from the University of Auckland in 1990. He worked as a process engineer for Sony (Audio Electronics) and Hewlett-Packard (Semiconductor LED) for 3 years prior to his post-graduate studies at the ANU where he obtained a Masters in theoretical physics, and a PhD in experimental physics. He was awarded the Australian Institute of Physics Bragg Medal and the ANU Crawford Prize for his PhD in 1999. He was an Alexander von Humboldt fellow at the Erlangen-Nürnberg Universität in 2000 and a CNRS visiting professor at Paris University in 2007. He was awarded the 2003 British Council Eureka Prize for inspiring science (Quantum Teleportation) and the 2006 UNSW Eureka Prize for innovative research (Quantum Cryptography). Ping Koy was the chief scientist and co-founder of QuintessenceLabs Pty. Ltd, a spin-off company of his group that commercialises quantum communication technology.

Ping Koy’s research interests include quantum optics, optical metrology, nonlinear optics and quantum information. Within the Centre, he manages the ANU node and is the quantum communication work package leader. His research covers quantum key distribution, quantum memory, quantum repeater and optical quantum information processing. He has published more than 200 scientific articles with more than 35 papers appearing in Physical Review Letters, Science and the Nature suite journals. His research expertise is in the field of quantum optics and metrology.

**Ping Koy Lam** [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_of_the_Australian_Academy_of_Science "Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science") is an Australian scientist and Professor of Physics at the [Australian National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_National_University "Australian National University") in [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra "Canberra"). He is currently an [Australian Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Research_Council "Australian Research Council") Australian Laureate Fellow and a work package director and program manager in the ARC Centre for Quantum Computer and Communication Technology.[[1]](#cite_note-1) For his PhD thesis in 1999 he was awarded the Australian Institute of Physics Bragg Medal.[[2]](#cite_note-auto-2) He was awarded the 2003 British Council [Eureka Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eureka_Prize "Eureka Prize") for inspiring science ([quantum teleportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_teleportation "Quantum teleportation")) and the 2006 UNSW [Eureka Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eureka_Prize "Eureka Prize") for innovative research ([quantum cryptography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_cryptography "Quantum cryptography")).[[2]](#cite_note-auto-2)

He researches [quantum optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_optics "Quantum optics"), optical [metrology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_metrology "Quantum metrology"), [nonlinear optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonlinear_optics "Nonlinear optics") and [quantum information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_information "Quantum information"). His highly cited research includes pioneering work in quantum memory, and optical [quantum information processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_information_science "Quantum information science").

In May 2020 he was elected fellow of the [Australian Academy of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Academy_of_Science "Australian Academy of Science").[[3]](#cite_note-3)

args.summary: Ping Koy Lam is an Australian physicist and Professor of Physics at the Australian National University (ANU) in Canberra. Born in Penang, Malaysia, he earned his education from the Australian National University and the University of Auckland. He is an Australian Research Council Australian Laureate Fellow and a program manager in the ARC Centre for Quantum Computer and Communication Technology. His research focuses on quantum optics, optical metrology, nonlinear optics, and quantum information, with highly cited work in quantum memory and optical quantum information processing. He received the AIP Bragg Medal for his PhD thesis in 1999, the 2003 British Council Eureka Prize for quantum teleportation, the 2006 UNSW Eureka Prize for quantum cryptography, and the AIP Alan Walsh Medal in 2014. In May 2020, he was elected a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science (FAA). He has held positions at ANU, Laboratoire Kastler-Brossel, and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg.

# A Quantum Leap for Communications

Thu, 10/22/2020 - 12:00

0%

*Space-based quantum communications startup SpeQtral is bringing future-proof security to the commercial world, says co-founder Mr Lum Chune Yang.*

---

Today, a range of futuristic technologies are being developed based on quantum phenomena—the ways that particles of matter and light behave and interact with each other. These technologies enable operations to be performed more accurately and efficiently than ever before.

Quantum-based technologies can also address one of the greatest security threats that we are facing today—the routine wiretapping by third parties of data transmitted over fibre optics. Even when the data is encrypted, public-key cryptography protocols used in secure data transmission are based on inherently breakable mathematical algorithms.

Fortunately, a method exists to keep malicious actors and eavesdroppers at bay. Called quantum key distribution (QKD), it uses the fundamental properties of quantum mechanics to transfer information between two entities.

“With QKD, keys delivered are tamper-proof and no progress in conventional computing or quantum computing would be able to break these encryption schemes,” says Mr Lum Chune Yang, co-founder and CEO of [SpeQtral](https://speqtral.space/), a startup that uses satellite-based QKD to enable the next generation of secure communication networks.

## The Only Constant is Change

A lifelong fascination with physics began during Mr Lum’s teenage years when he read a book about Einstein’s Theory of Relativity. “I just couldn’t wrap my head around the fact that the speed of light is constant in all reference frames and that time and length ‘changes’ in order to keep the speed of light constant,” he shared.

After an early stint in quantum research and a career in the satellite telecommunications industry, Mr Lum spotted an opportunity for commercial applications of satellite-based QKD. Spun off from the Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT), a Research Centre of Excellence hosted by the National University of Singapore (NUS), SpeQtral is based on the research of Mr Lum’s co-founder, CQT Principal Investigator and NUS Associate Professor Alexander Ling. “Alex’s research work is what the company is founded upon. As for me, I bring the space, business and telecommunication expertise,” Mr Lum said.

The startup is developing space-based quantum communication networks for the global delivery of secure encryption keys, and is commercialising satellite QKD technology developed at CQT. QKD satellites are able to establish a quantum-secured channel to the receiving parties and automate the secure delivery of symmetric encryption keys used for encrypting communication networks.

“These encryption keys, which are generated via a quantum process, are inherently random and use information embedded in particles of light (photons) as the bits (1s and 0s) that form the encryption keys,” Mr Lum explained. “Importantly, this method of key distribution is tamper-proof, because if an eavesdropper tries to steal the information, the quantum states carried by the photons would be disrupted and the eavesdropper’s presence would be revealed.”

Not only does quantum-based encryption technology provide safer communications in the present, it also provides an insurance against being cracked by a future quantum computer or conventional computers using better algorithms. “Symmetric encryption also has forward security, meaning no advances in conventional or quantum computational methods would be able to compromise encryption using this method,” Mr Lum said.

## Extending the Range of Quantum Key Distribution

Today, QKD technology can already be deployed over optical fibre networks, but existing options are limited to approximately 50-100 kilometres in range. “SpeQtral is focused on bridging the long distance key distribution problem. CQT has developed and demonstrated miniature and rugged quantum light sources that can be deployed on small satellites—shoe-box sized satellites called CubeSats,” he said.

“These quantum satellites would be able to distribute encryption keys to anywhere on Earth, and essentially act as an overlay to any telecommunications network by delivering these keys to encrypt existing high bandwidth data communications links,” Mr Lum said. To date, SpeQtral is the only team that is building on technology heritage from successful in-space demonstrations of quantum light sources on CubeSats.

The startup has received US$1.9 million in seed funding in a round led by Space Capital, the venture fund of space investor and operator, Space Angels. Space Angels also participated in the round, as did Shasta Ventures, Golden Gate Ventures and SGInnovate. The co-founders will use the capital to expand the team, open offices in Singapore and the United States, and kick off a commercially-focused space-to-ground CubeSat quantum communication demonstration mission.

“We think that satellite QKD could essentially be integrated with telecommunications networks. We are looking to secure government and defence communication networks, as well as commercial telecommunication networks, and both these market segment would be a bit different in terms of adoption,” Mr Lum said.

## To Infinity and Beyond

While Mr Lum is confident about the commercial value of quantum technology, he remains conscious of the lack of awareness among investors and the general public. “Many investors still do not know about quantum technologies and quantum communications specifically.”

“In addition, there is a lack of understanding of the potential threats to our communication networks and the need to implement new methods. Therefore, educating and informing the broader industry at scale would be an important task for us,” Mr Lum said.

Hiring talent also remains a challenge for SpeQtral, Mr Lum said, but he is thankful that both CQT and SGInnovate have built up a large network of Deep Tech expertise from which SpeQtral has been able to access.

“Besides supporting us in fundraising, SGInnovate also connected us with potential partners and customers, and gave us exposure in public forums. Having a Singapore Government-backed fund like SGInnovate as an investor was a vote of confidence in SpeQtral, especially when in discussions with international parties,” Mr Lum said.

This article from SGInnovate (dated October 22, 2020) profiles SpeQtral, a Singapore-based space-based quantum communications startup that is commercializing satellite-based Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) technology. SpeQtral was spun off from the Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT) at the National University of Singapore (NUS), founded by CEO Lum Chune Yang (who brings space, business, and telecom expertise) and co-founder/Principal Investigator Assoc. Prof. Alexander Ling (whose research forms the company's foundation).

QKD uses the fundamental properties of quantum mechanics to transfer encryption keys between two entities in a tamper-proof manner. Unlike traditional public-key cryptography, QKD-based encryption cannot be broken by advances in conventional or quantum computing. The keys are generated via a quantum process using photons, and any eavesdropping attempt disrupts the quantum states, revealing the intrusion.

SpeQtral focuses on overcoming the range limitation of fiber-based QKD (currently limited to 50-100 km) by deploying miniature, rugged quantum light sources on small satellites called CubeSats. These quantum satellites can distribute encryption keys anywhere on Earth, acting as an overlay to existing telecommunications networks. SpeQtral is the only team building on heritage from successful in-space demonstrations of quantum light sources on CubeSats.

The startup raised US$1.9 million in seed funding led by Space Capital, with participation from Space Angels, Shasta Ventures, Golden Gate Ventures, and SGInnovate. The funds will be used to expand the team, open offices in Singapore and the US, and launch a commercially-focused space-to-ground CubeSat quantum communication demonstration mission. Target markets include government/defense and commercial telecommunications networks.

Challenges include lack of investor and public awareness about quantum technologies and the need for new security methods, as well as hiring talent. SGInnovate has supported SpeQtral through fundraising connections, partner introductions, and public exposure.

args.summary:
SpeQtral is a company focused on securing global networks in the quantum era by combining space-based quantum key distribution (QKD) with terrestrial fibre networks. Their roadmap includes: Quantum-Safe Terrestrial Networks using fibre-based QKD for metropolitan networks (2024), a Quantum-Safe Global Network using satellites to generate and transmit un-hackable symmetric quantum keys over long distances (2025), and a Global Quantum Fabric integrating hardware and software systems (2026). 

Key milestones include: SpooQy-1 satellite deployment from the ISS in 2019 (producing entangled photon sources in orbit), point-to-point fibre QKD deployments with Toshiba (2020-2022), building a quantum communications network across Singapore (2023), and a planned quantum satellite launch (2025).

The company addresses the quantum threat of bad actors intercepting encrypted data today for future decryption. Investors include Xora, Golden Gate Ventures, SGInnovate, Space Angels, TIS INTEC, and Shasta Ventures. Recent news includes free-space quantum communications trials (July 2025), an MoU with SES (March 2025), an MoU with Toshiba and ST Engineering (September 2024), and collaboration with MAS on quantum security trials (August 2024).

<webpage_content>
[Satellite Missions Catalogue](/satellite-missions?Mission+type=EO)

# SOCRATES (Space Optical Communications Research Advanced Technology Satellite)

|
|

Mission complete

|

## Quick facts

#### Overview

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Mission type | EO |
| Agency | NICT |
| Mission status | Mission complete |
| Launch date | 24 May 2014 |
| End of life date | 24 May 2019 |
| Measurement domain | Atmosphere |
| CEOS EO Handbook | [See SOCRATES (Space Optical Communications Research Advanced Technology Satellite) summary](https://database.eohandbook.com/database/missionsummary.aspx?missionID=1380&utm_source=eoportal&utm_content=socrates) |

## SOCRATES (Space Optical Communications Research Advanced Technology Satellite)

**[Spacecraft](#spacecraft)     [Launch](#launch)    [Mission Status](#mission-status)     [Experiments](#experiments)    [Optical Ground Station](#ogs)    [References](#references)**

SOCRATES is a microsatellite mission of NICT (National Institute of Information and Communications Technology), Koganei, Tokyo, Japan. The overall objective is to demonstrate and validate the operation of **SOTA** (Small Optical TrAnsponder), a laser communication system in space. The goal is to experiment with QKD (Quantum Key Distribution) techniques and to foster the application free-space optical communications (higher data rates than RF communications) in microsatellites and eventually in nanosatellites. [1)](#foot1%29) [2)](#foot2%29) [3)](#foot3%29) [4)](#foot4%29)

SOTA is controlled via the TT&C (Tracking Telemetry and Command) link from the TT&C RF ground station. The laser communication experiment is conducted between SOTA and OGS (Optical Ground Station) located at NICT. The establishment of 10 Mbit/s communication links is the main mission of SOCRATES (measurement of the laser beam propagation through turbulent atmosphere at difference of wavelengths). By using the laser communication links, the propagation data at wavelengths of 1.5 µm and 1.06 µm can be measured.

![Figure 1: Overview of the SOCRATES mission configuration (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto18.jpeg)

Figure 1: Overview of the SOCRATES mission configuration (image credit: NICT)

![Figure 2: Illustration of the SOCRATES spacecraft (image credit: AES)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto17.jpeg)

Figure 2: Illustration of the SOCRATES spacecraft (image credit: AES)

  

## Spacecraft

The SOCRATES microsatellite, developed for NICT by AES (Advanced Engineering Services Co.,Ltd.), Tsukuba, Japan, employs the small satellite standard bus. The objective of the mission is to demonstrate the operation of the small standard satellite bus. [5)](#foot5%29) [6)](#foot6%29)

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Mission success | - Confirmation of the most basic components operation capabilities consisting of satellite bus in orbit. - Deployment of two solar array panels and telemetry communication between space and ground. |
| Full success | - Confirmation of all components of the bus will operate properly in orbit. - To generate enough electrical power and supply for the satellite to survive. - Implementation of direction change to the Sun by three axis stabilized attitude control. |
| Extra success | - In addition to normal operations of mission equipment, contribution for experiment through stable attitude control and power based on the needs of users. - Establishment of the automatic operation system (it means that we can operate it full automatic without manual control). |
Table 1: Success criteria of the SOCRATES mission

The standard bus is comprised of the following subsystems:

1) STR (Structure)

2) EPS (Electrical Power Subsystem) with PCU (Power Control Unit), SAP (Solar Array Panel) and BAT (Battery).

3) DHS (Data Handling Subsystem) with OBC (OnBoard Computer)

4) RF communication subsystem, consisting of SANT (S-band antenna), SCPL (S-band Coupler), SDIP (S-band Diplexer), and STRX (S-band Transponder).

5) ACS (Attitude Control Subsystem), consisting of MTQ (Magnetic Torquer), WHL (Wheel), DSS (Digital Sun Sensor), CSS (Coarse Sun Sensor), MAGS (Magnetic Sensors), VSGA (Vibrating Structure Gyroscope Assembly), GPSA (GPS Antenna), GPSC (GPS Coupler), and GPSR (GPS Receiver).

6) INT (integration hardware), consisting of TS (Temperature Sensors), HTR (Heater), and HNS (Harness).

![Figure 3: Functional block diagram of SOCRATES (image credit: AES)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto16.jpeg)

Figure 3: Functional block diagram of SOCRATES (image credit: AES)

JAXA and MEC (Meisei Electric Company) developed MESA (Micro Earth Sensor Assembly) applying COTS based 4 thermopile arrays. The size of MESA is 40 x 40 x 50 mm excluding flange with a mass of 137 g. MESA provides 2D attitude information with an accuracy of <1º. MESA is a technology demonstration device on SOCRATES. [7)](#foot7%29)

MESA is not included in onboard realtime attitude control system, because it has no flight heritage yet. In order to evaluate performance of MESA, output of each detector and relating raw data during earth attitude control mode of SOCRATES such as sun pointing mode or Earth pointing mode are obtained.

MESA data are downloaded in order to compare with the data of the star tracker, STR. With evaluating attitude obtained by MESA and STR, it is confirmed that the accuracy of attitude determination with MESA is generally less than 1º.

![Figure 4: Left: Assembly of MESA; right: photo of the MESA instrument (image credit: MEC, JAXA, AES)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto15.jpeg)

Figure 4: Left: Assembly of MESA; right: photo of the MESA instrument (image credit: MEC, JAXA, AES)

![Figure 5: Overview of some spacecraft elements (image credit: AES)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto14.jpeg)

Figure 5: Overview of some spacecraft elements (image credit: AES)

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Spacecraft mass | 48 kg |
| External dimensions of the spacecraft | W 496 x D495 x H485 mm (SAP is folded during launch) |
| Power generation | ~100 W (nominal), 120 W (max), use of SAP deployment mechanism |
| ACS (Attitude Control Subsystem) | Three axis stabilized attitude control, solar pointing control, earth pointing control |
| RF communications | S-band |
Table 2: Specification parameters of SOCRATES

## Launch

The SOCRATES microsatellite was launched as a secondary payload on May 24, 2014 (03:05 UTC) on a H-IIA vehicle from TNSC (Tanegashima Space Center), Japan. The launch provider was MHI (Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd.). The primary payload on this flight was the ALOS-2 (Daichi-2) spacecraft of JAXA. [8)](#foot8%29)

The secondary missions manifested on the ALOS-2 mission by JAXA were: [9)](#foot9%29)

• Rising-2, a cooperative microsatellite (43 kg) project of Tohoku University (Sendai) and Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan.

• UNIFORM-1 (University International Formation Mission-1), of Wakayama University, Wakayama, Japan.

• SOCRATES (Space Optical Communications Research Advanced Technology Satellite), a microsatellite (48 kg) mission of NICT (National Institute of Information and Communications Technology), Koganei, Japan.

• SPROUT (Space Research on Unique Technology), a nanosatellite of ~7 kg of Nihon University, Tokyo, Japan.

**Orbit:** Sun-synchronous near-circular sub-recurrent orbit, altitude = 628 km, inclination = 97.9º, period = 97.4 minutes, LSDN (Local Sun time on Descending Node) = 12:00 hours ± 15 min.

![Figure 6: Photo of the secondary payloads integrated on the adapter ring of the second stage (image credit: JAXA)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto13.jpeg)

Figure 6: Photo of the secondary payloads integrated on the adapter ring of the second stage (image credit: JAXA)

---

## Mission Status

• July 11, 2017: NICT developed the world's smallest and lightest quantum-communication transmitter (SOTA) onboard the microsatellite SOCRATES. The project succeeded in the demonstration of the first quantum-communication experiment from space, receiving information from the satellite in a single-photon regime in an optical ground station in Koganei city. SOTA has a mass of 6 kg and its size is 17.8 cm length, 11.4 cm width and 26.8 cm height. It transmits a laser signal to the ground at a rate of 10 Mbit/s from an altitude of 600 km at a speed of 7 km/s. The project succeeded in correctly detecting the communication signal from SOTA moving at this fast speed. This is a major step toward building a global long-haul and truly-secure satellite communication network. [10)](#foot10%29) [11)](#foot11%29)

- As a result of this research, NICT demonstrated that satellite quantum communication can be implemented with small low-cost satellites, which makes it possible to many research institutions and companies to use this key technology. It is an achievement that opens a new page in the development future global communication networks, being a big boost to the space industry.

• Sept./Oct. 2016: The SOTA (Small Optical TrAnsponder) lasercom terminal onboard the SOCRATES satellite has been operated by NICT for around two years. In this time, all the goals of the mission have been achieved, including up to 10 Mbit/s downlinks using two different wavelengths and apertures, verification of coarse and fine tracking of the OGS (Optical Ground Station) beacon, space-to-ground transmission of pseudo-random sequences and images from the on-board-camera as well as preloaded samples, and experiments with different error correcting codes. At the moment, two extra-success phases of the mission are ongoing: interoperability with other international OGS and basic experiments on space QKD (Quantum Key Distribution). [12)](#foot12%29)

• The SOCRATES spacecraft and its payload are operating nominally in the spring of 2016. [13)](#foot13%29)

- The space-to-ground laser communication experiments have been conducted with SOTA. Atmospheric turbulence causes signal fadings and becomes an issue to be solved in satellite-to-ground laser communication links. Therefore, as error-correcting functions, a Reed-Solomon (RS) code and a Low-Density Generator Matrix (LDGM) code are implemented in the communication system onboard the SOTA. Almost all of the success criteria have been met. It was confirmed that even stronger receiving power than predicted by the previous optical link design was received in the experiment. Also, a comparison of the optical link design and approximately ±2 dB under the Rytov approximation showed similar results. The data recovery with an error-correcting code from the packet loss due to atmospheric fluctuations and tracking errors was also confirmed. [14)](#foot14%29)

- In 2015, the first links between the SOCRATES microsatellite atLEO and an OGS (Optical Ground Station) in Europe has been established with two different wavelengths and at several OGS apertures (collaboration between CNES, NICT, and Geoazur). Acquisition and tracking were successfully performed during the various passes. Basic data such as power fluctuation, frequency spectrum, telecom data and BER were obtained. The telecom link quality is almost good at 1.5 m and 0.4 m OGS aperture, and it is limited at 0.2 m OGS aperture. Optical power levels detected at OGS and at SOTA match well with theoretical estimation. [15)](#foot15%29)

• July, 2015: NICT started experimental verification of optical satellite communications using SOTA (Small Optical TrAnsponder) last September. A practical fading generator with respect to collected experimental data has been developed for communications system design. The fading generator consists of two components: fade level and noise variance generators based on model fitting the corrected data into theoretical atmospheric turbulence distribution. [16)](#foot16%29)

- The OPTical communications working group (OPT) of the SLS (Space Link Services) in CCSDS (Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems) is in charge of optical satellite communication systems. The low complexity system with OOK (On-Off Keying) modulation is one of the categories for physical layer standardization by SLS-OPT. The OOK based IM/DD (Intensity Modulation with Direct Detection) format is preferred to enable a simple, robust, and cost-effective setup for optical satellite communications, especially in LEO (Low Earth Orbit) satellite applications. The practical system performances must be evaluated to edit the Green/Blue Books.  
In optical satellite communications, an atmospheric turbulence affects received signals. Burst errors and tracking difficulties due to fading seriously degrade performances. Therefore, it is desirable to model a practical fading channel by reflecting accurate statistics with atmospheric turbulence-induced signal fade based on measurements.

- NICT initiated an R&D effort of SOTA (Small Optical TrAnsponder) for LEOs to demonstrate the attractive features of optical technology in the frame of the SOCRATES (Space Optical Communication Research Advanced TEchnology Satellite) project. The SOTA measurement campaign started in September 2014, and different test scenarios have been conducted to understand characteristics of optical satellite channel. The experimental data obtained by SOTA campaign has been utilized for the channel modeling. The fading generator based on the measurements has been developed using model fitting technique. The system performances in optical satellite channel can be easily simulated by implementing in the fading generator.

- **Evaluation of SOTA downlink signals:** The SOTA measurement campaign has been performed in order to collect downlink signals with different data formats such as image data and Pseudo-random Noise (PN) sequences. The project focuses on the format of PN sequence with the period of 215-1 called "PRBS 15" due to a known data sequence. The specifications of the downlink signals are listed in Table [3](#YcBoL12beHerb). The data collection system including SOTA receiver and digital storage oscilloscope (DSO) as shown in Figure [7](#rCCoL16Herb). The received optical satellite downlink signal is passed to APD (Avalanche Photo Diode) to convert into an electrical one, followed by loopback modules including two LPFs (Low-Pass Filters), A/D and D/A converters. The output loopback electrical signals are stored in DSO at a sampling frequency of 50 MHz in time interval of every 4 s. A length of single snapshot is 4e6 samples (0.08 s) due to the limitation of DSO. There are 456 PN sequences in a single path.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Wavelength | 1549 nm |
| Transmit power (average) | 34.8 nW |
| Tx antenna diameter | 8.1 nm |
| Modulation | NRZ-OOK (Non-Return to Zero/On-Off Keying) |
| Modulation symbol rate | 10 Msps |
| Propagation distance | 600 - 1000 km |
| RX antenna diameter | 1 m |
| Photodetection technique | IM/DD |
| RX detector | InGaAs APD (Avalanche Photo Diode) |
Table 3: Specification of SOTA downlink communications

![Figure 7: SOTA offline receiver for PN sequence (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto12.jpeg)

Figure 7: SOTA offline receiver for PN sequence (image credit: NICT)

![Figure 8: The collected snapshots (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto11.jpeg)

Figure 8: The collected snapshots (image credit: NICT)

The collected snapshots in two channel environments, falloff and strong signals, are shown in Figure [8](#ECCoL1276Herb) (a) and (b), respectively. 24 PN sequences are continuously sampled in a snapshot. The stored electrical signals in DSO are demodulated by offline receiver as shown in Figure [9](#IHCoL13c9Herb). A sliding PN correlator finds the optimum start point of each PN sequence. A TTL (Time Tracking Loop) tracks timing shift due to oscillator and Doppler shift. The synchronized signals are integrated over its oversampling ratio of 5 samples and dumped. The dumped symbols are determined as "0" or "1" by hard decision, and then BERs (Bit Rate Errors) over each PN period are calculated. In subsequent discussion, we analyze the collected data in a single path, since available data is obtained on a day only. The BER distribution during the single path is calculated by plotting BER of each PN period versus electrical signal power as shown in Figure [10](#pOCoL1212Herb). There are 28 % of error free PN sequences more than the signal power of 1.1. The electric power is calculated by averaging square of the amplitude over PN period. The obtained histogram is shown in Figure [11](#OXCoL1172Herb). The experimental power distribution plotted with the blue circles does not indicate a smooth line due to the small number of collected samples.

![Figure 9: SOTA offline receiver for PN sequence (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_Auto10.jpeg)

Figure 9: SOTA offline receiver for PN sequence (image credit: NICT)

![Figure 10: BER distribution for the single path (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_AutoF.jpeg)

Figure 10: BER distribution for the single path (image credit: NICT)

![Figure 11: Power distribution for the single path (image credit: NICT)](/api/cms/documents/163813/2864604/Socrates_AutoE.jpeg)

Figure 11: Power distribution for the single path (image credit: NICT)

- **System demonstration:** The fading generator is implemented as a part of system simulator as shown in Figure 7. The block diagram consists of OOK modulator/demodulator, convolutional interleaver/deinterleaver, LDPC (Low Density Parity Check) encoder/decoder, and fading generator. The system specifications are listed in Table 2. The LDPC code according to CCSDS 131.0-B-1 6) is adopted to correct errors due to fading. The input to the LDPC decoder is soft decision demodulated signals to improve coding gain obtained by a MAP (Maximum A posteriori Possibility) decoding algorithm called modified BCJR algorithm. The soft decision threshold value is heuristically found to obtain the minimum BER. The interleaver also plays an important role in communications in fading channel, since the spreading out of burst errors caused by fading is accomplished. The deinterleaved soft decision signals are suitable for the LDPC decoder. Note that the lowest value of the noise variance generator is limited to 0 dB, since the receiver can not be synchronized with the incoming signals under the SNR of 0 dB. To evaluate performances, the system is demonstrated by implementing a signal processing worksystem (SPW). [17)](#foot17%29)

The distributions obtained from the fading generator are shown in Figure [12](#znCoL132Herb). ## Sensor Complement

### SOTA (Small Optical TrAnsponder)

After the successful laser communication demonstrations between space and the optical ground stations in NICT and other international stations, using LUCE (Laser Utilizing Communications Equipment) onboard OICETS (Optical Interorbit Communications Engineering Test Satellite), NICT initiated its R&D activities of SOTA for microsatellites within the frame of the SOCRATES (Space Optical Communication Research Advanced Technology Satellite) project. [18)](#foot18%29) [19)](#foot19%29) [20)](#foot20%29) [21)](#foot21%29) [22)](#foot22%29) [23)](#foot23%29)

The objectives of SOTA are:

• On orbit acquisition, tracking and communication performance verification of the small optical terminal

• To acquire propagation data through the atmosphere at various wavelengths

• Communication quality measurement

• To determine the effect of coding on the communication quality

• Basic experiment for QKD (Quantum Key Distribution)

• Experiments with international OGSs (Optical Ground Stations)

• Command operation by optical link (future)

• Link experiment with aircraft (future)

• Link experiment with satellite (future).

The SOTA instrumentation was designed and developed at NICT in cooperation with NEC Corporation, NEC Toshiba Space Systems, Ltd.

The development of SOTA started based on the proposed **BBM** (Bread Board Model) from an industry team. The model consisted of an optical part (**SOTA-OPT**) and a controller (**SOTA-CONT**). In the optical part, two AQD (Acquisition Quadrant Detectors) and for tracking (T-QD), four laser transmitters and a 45 mm diameter receiving optics with a FQD (Fine-pointing Quadrant Detector), FPM (Fine Pointing Mechanism), and an APD (Avalanche Photo Diode) were installed on the optical bench.

The optical bench was mounted on an Elevation (El) actuator and Azimuth (Az) rotational table. These tables were COTS (Commercial off-the-Shelf) devices which needed some modifications for space application. The main design parameters are listed in the Table [4](#bhj9E1280Herb). ### SOTA PFM (Proto-Flight Model)

Major modifications of the SOTA PFM design from BBM and EM design are:

• The width of the 2-axis gimbal is reduced to 177 mm

• The beam expender in the receiving optics is replaced with a Cassegrain telescope which is very small and of low mass. And the diameter of telescope is increased to 5 cm.

• The acquisition QD and the tracking QD are replaced by one detector, referred to as T-QD, with an increased aperture diameter of 2.3 cm.

The SOTA has four transmitters (TX1~4) which operate at 980 nm (TX1), 800 nm band (TX2 and 3) and 1550 nm (TX4). TX1 and TX4 transmit an optical signal which is selectable from data sources of PN,; the image data and telemetry data of SOTA have data rates of 10Mbit/s and 1Mbit/s, respectively. TX2 and TX 3 are used for basic quantum measurements for satellite quantum key distribution. The light from these transmitters is linearly polarized.

The up-link signal is asynchronous NRZ whose carrier frequency is 40 kHz and the signal bandwidth is 1 kHz. The wavelength of the uplink is 1064 nm. The optical signal of the uplink is received by the receiving optics with an aperture of 5 cm and focused on a multimode fiber which is connected to a PIN photo diode in the SOTA-CONT.

Table [6](#4Ll9E11f4Herb) gives a performance summary of the SOTA PFM. The acquisition, tracking and pointing functions are realized by a 2-axes gimbal, FPM and related sensors. The angular range is expanded to ±50º in both the Az and El axis. The estimated fundamental frequency is more than 60 Hz. Micro-stepping motors are used to drive the 2-axes gimbal with a minimum angular resolution of 0.001125º/pulse.

The power consumption of the SOTA depends on the operational modes. A minimum power consumption is expected as 28.1 W with only the TX1 transmitter in operation. When TX1 and a receiver are operating simultaneously, the required power reaches 39.5 W.

The total mass of SOTA is estimated to be ~ 6.2 kg. The size of SOTA-OPT is 177.5 W x 130 D x 264 H (mm). By selecting the direction of the SOTA FOV, this size will be acceptable for the satellite bus.

## OGS (Optical Ground Station)

NICT (National Institute of Information and Communications Technology) constructed the OGS for the satellite laser communication experiment at HQs in Koganei, Tokyo. The core facility of the OGS is the Cassegrain reflector telescope with 1 meter aperture; the tracking and pointing performance is enough for LEO satellite support. The new OGS is dedicated for the SOTA/SOCRATES experiment. [24)](#foot24%29)

The primary mirror is a concave parabola while the secondary mirror is a hyperbola layout. The top ring with secondary mirror support structure is supported with a truss structure on the primary mirror cell. A bulk structure with primary mirror cell is mounted to the altitude-azimuth mount of the telescope system. To shield the system from wind and unwanted external light, a thin shield plate can be equipped on the truss and support structure. The focusing of the telescope system is executed by adjustment of distance between the primary mirror and secondary mirrors. The distance between the primary mirror cell and the top ring, which supports the secondary mirror assembly, is monitored by a laser displacement meter. The monitoring of the laser displacement meter provides accurate reproducibility of the telescope system focusing by the secondary mirror displacement.

The telescope system has one Cassegrain focus, two Nathmys foci, and two Coude foci, which is available with change of light path by flat mirrors. The telescope system has a collimator lens to provide the Coude focus far from telescope main optics. The design wavelengths are: 1.550 µm, 1.064 µm, and 0.532 µm, which is the wavelength of laser light sources for our application. The 0.532 µm is for the satellite laser ranging experiment. The Coude path is designed with no focus point on the light path, because the satellite laser ranging will use a pulse laser with large output power.

The following options are available for the provision of tracking data:

In AET mode, the tracking operation can be automatically started immediately after receiving the AET table via LAN or IP. The required tracking and pointing performance is confirmed in tracking test of the AJISAI or ENVISAT satellites and the SOCRATES/SOTA experiment. The Experimental Geodetic Satellite AJISAI is a bright satellite, reflecting sunlight with about 116 minutes orbital period and its orbit is determined precisely and opened. With a tracking test of AJISAI, the tracking performance test and adjustment including debugging is executed. Figure [22](#lcWUO118dHerb) is an example of tracking data in the SOCRATES/SOTA experiment operation. The graph shows that the tracking error of SOTA/SOCRATES tracking is less than five arc seconds. Furthermore, the small jitter during satellite tracking is a great advantage of this telescope. During the tracking test of the AJISAI satellite, we cannot find noticeable short period jitter or an abrupt jump of the satellite image which is often found during the visual observation of a LEO satellite or the Space Station by using a telescope for astronomical utility.
